<!-- example-1: body_md -->
\label{exm:StandardModels}
    In what follows, we define a Hessian domain by an analytic
    potential function~$\psi$ on a domain in~$\mathbb{R}^n$.\\
    (1)~Let~$c<0$.\\
    \quad $\mathcal{S}^{n}(c):=\mathbb{R}^{n}$,
    \quad $\psi:=
    -\frac{1}{c}\log(1+e^{\theta^1}+\cdots+e^{\theta^n}).$\\
    (2)~For~$k=0,\ldots, n$,\\
    \quad $\mathcal{R}^{n,k}(0):=\mathbb{R}^{n}$,
    \quad $\psi:=
    \frac{1}{2}(\theta^{1})^2+\cdots+\frac{1}{2}(\theta^{k})^2
    +e^{\theta^{k+1}}+\cdots+e^{\theta^n}.$\\
    (3)~Let~$c>0$.\\
    (3-i)~$\mathcal{H}^{n}(c):=\left\{(\theta^1,\ldots,\theta^n)\in\mathbb{R}^{n}~:~
    e^{\theta^1}+\cdots+e^{\theta^n}<1\right\}$,\\
    \quad $\psi:=-\frac{1}{c}\log(1-e^{\theta^1}-\cdots-e^{\theta^n}).$\\
    (3-ii)~$\mathcal{H}^{n,\mathrm{H}}(c):=\left\{(\theta^1,\ldots,\theta^n)\in
    \left(-\frac{\pi}{2},\frac{\pi}{2}\right)\times\mathbb{R}^{n-1}~:~
    e^{\theta^2}+\cdots+e^{\theta^n}<\cos\theta^1\right\}$,\\
    \quad $\psi:=-\frac{1}{c}\log(\cos\theta^1-e^{\theta^2}-\cdots-e^{\theta^n}).$\\
    (3-iii)~For~$k=1,\ldots,n$,\\
    \quad $\mathcal{H}^{n,k}(c):=\left\{(\theta^1,\ldots,\theta^n)\in\mathbb{R}^{n}~:~
    \theta^{1}+\frac{1}{2}(\theta^{2})^2+\cdots+\frac{1}{2}(\theta^{k})^2
    +e^{\theta^{k+1}}+\cdots+e^{\theta^n}<0\right\}$,\\
    \quad $\psi:=-\frac{1}{c}\log\left(-\theta^{1}-\frac{1}{2}(\theta^{2})^2-\cdots
    -\frac{1}{2}(\theta^{k})^2
    -e^{\theta^{k+1}}-\cdots-e^{\theta^n}\right).$
<!-- end example-1 -->
<!-- proposition-1: body_md -->
The above examples are 
    convex maximal Hessian domains of constant Hessian sectional curvature.
<!-- end proposition-1 -->
<!-- definition-1: body_md -->
We call the Hessian manifolds defined in 
    Example~\ref{exm:StandardModels} 
    the \textit{standard models} of constant Hessian sectional curvature.
<!-- end definition-1 -->
<!-- theorem-1: body_md -->
\label{mthm:LocalEmbedding}
    For any connected and simply connected Hessian manifold
    with constant Hessian sectional curvature,
    there exists a local diffeomorphism preserving the Hessian structures
    to one of the standard models.
<!-- end theorem-1 -->
<!-- proposition-2: body_md -->
\label{prop:QuotientHessian1}
    Let~$N$ be a~$2n$-dimensional K\"{a}hler~manifold
    equipped with an effective, proper and Hamiltonian action
    of an~$n$-dimensional connected abelian Lie group~$\mathbb{A}$.
    Then, for~$N^\circ_{\mathbb{A}}:=\{p\in N~:~ \mathbb{A}_p=\{e\}\}$,
    the quotient manifold~$M^\circ_{\mathbb{A}}:=N^\circ_{\mathbb{A}}/\mathbb{A}$
    naturally carries a Hessian structure,
    where~$\mathbb{A}_p$ denotes the isotropy subgroup at~$p\in N.$
<!-- end proposition-2 -->
<!-- theorem-2: body_md -->
\label{mthm:Correspondence}
    In Proposition~\ref{prop:QuotientHessian1}, 
    if, in addition,~$N$ is connected, 
    simply connected, complete, 
    and has constant holomorphic sectional curvature, 
    then the quotient manifold~$M^\circ_{\mathbb{A}}$ 
    is a convex maximal Hessian domain of constant Hessian sectional curvature.
    Conversely, every convex maximal Hessian domain 
    of constant Hessian sectional curvature can be obtained 
    as such a quotient, up to isomorphism.
<!-- end theorem-2 -->
<!-- definition-2: body_md -->
(1)~For an affine connection~$\nabla$ on~$M$
    and a Riemannian metric~$g$ on~$M$,
    a triple~$(M, \nabla,g)$ is called a \textit{Hessian manifold}
    if~$N$ is flat, that is, its curvature and torsion both vanish,
    and, around every point~$p\in M$,
    there exists a smooth function~$\psi$ such that
    $g=\nabla^2 \psi$.
    We call~$\psi$ a \textit{(Hessian) potential} of~$g$.\\
    (2)~A Hessian manifold~$(U,\nabla,g)$
    is called a \textit{Hessian domain}
    if~$U$ is a domain, that is, a connected open subset
    of~$\mathbb{R}^{n}$,
    $\nabla$ coincides with the standard flat connection on~$\mathbb{R}^{n}$,
    and~$g$ admits a globally defined Hessian potential~$\psi$ on~$U$.
<!-- end definition-2 -->
<!-- fact-1: body_md -->
\label{fac:HessianCondition}
    The~$(\nabla, g)$ defines a Hessian structure
    if and only if~$\nabla g$ is symmetric in its three arguments.
    In particular, this is equivalent to
    \begin{equation*}
        Xg(Y,Z)-Yg(X,Z)=0
    \end{equation*}
    for any locally defined parallel vector fields
    $X, Y, Z$ on~$M$.
<!-- end fact-1 -->
<!-- note-1: body_md -->
Let~$(U,\nabla, g=\nabla^2\psi)$ be a Hessian domain.
    Then, the \textit{gradient map}:
    \begin{equation*}
        \nabla\psi:=\left(\frac{\partial \psi}{\partial \theta^1},\ldots, \frac{\partial \psi}{\partial \theta^n}\right)
        \colon U\rightarrow \mathbb{R}^{n}
    \end{equation*}
    is locally diffeomorphic and, if~$U$ is convex, 
    it is moreover a diffeomorphism.
<!-- end note-1 -->
<!-- definition-3: body_md -->
\label{def:DualChart}
    Let~$(U,\nabla, g=\nabla^2 \psi)$ be a convex Hessian domain.
    Then we define the 
    \textit{dual chart}~$(\eta_1,\ldots, \eta_n)$
    of the standard chart~$(\theta^1,\ldots, \theta^n)$
    by
    $\eta_i:=\frac{\partial \psi}{\partial \theta^i}$ ($i=1,\ldots, n$).
<!-- end definition-3 -->
<!-- definition-4: body_md -->
Let~$(M,\nabla,g)$ be a Hessian manifold.\\
    (1)~The \textit{difference tensor}~$\gamma$ is the~$(1,2)$-tensor field 
    defined by~$\gamma:=\nabla-\nabla^g$,
    where~$\nabla^g$ denotes the Levi-Civita connection of~$g$.\\
    (2)~The \textit{Hessian curvature tensor}~$Q$
    is the~$(1,3)$-tensor field defined by
    \begin{equation*}
        Q(X,Y,Z):=(\nabla_Y\gamma)(X,Z)
    \end{equation*}
    for any vector fields~$X, Y, Z$ on~$M$.\\
    (3)~Let~$S^2(TM)$ denote the symmetric square of~$TM$.
    For any~$p\in M$ and~$X,Y\in T_pM\setminus{0}$,
    the \textit{Hessian sectional curvature}~$q:S^2(TM)\rightarrow \mathbb{R}^{}$
    is defined by
    \begin{equation*}
        q(X\odot Y):=
        \frac{2g(X,Q(X,Y,Y))}
        {g(X,X)g(Y,Y)+g(X,Y)^2}.
    \end{equation*}
<!-- end definition-4 -->
<!-- fact-2: body_md -->
A Hessian manifold has
    constant Hessian sectional curvature~$c\in \mathbb{R}^{}$
    if and only if 
    \begin{equation*}
        Q_{iajb}=g\left(\frac{\partial }{\partial \theta^i},
        Q\left(\frac{\partial }{\partial \theta^a},\frac{\partial }{\partial \theta^j},
        \frac{\partial }{\partial \theta^b}\right)\right)=\frac{c}{2}(g_{ia}g_{jb}+g_{ib}g_{ja})
    \end{equation*}
    in any affine chart~$(\theta^1,\ldots,\theta^n)$.
<!-- end fact-2 -->
<!-- definition-5: body_md -->
Let~$(U,\nabla, g=\nabla^2\psi)$ be a convex Hessian domain,
    $\nabla \psi\colon U\rightarrow \mathbb{R}^{n}$ be
    the gradient map,
    and~$(\eta_1,\ldots, \eta_n)$ be the dual chart
    (Definition~\ref{def:DualChart}).\\
    (1)~
    The \textit{variance function}~$V\colon (\nabla\psi)(U)\rightarrow
    \operatorname{\mathrm{Sym}}(n,\mathbb{R}^{})$ is defined by:
    \begin{equation*}
        V_{ij}:=\frac{\partial^2\psi}{\partial\theta^i\partial\theta^j}
        \circ (\nabla\psi)^{-1}.
    \end{equation*}
    (2)~The variance function~$V$ is 
    said to be \textit{simple quadratic}
    if there exists some~$c\in\mathbb{R}^{}$ such that
    \begin{equation*}
        \frac{\partial^2V_{ij}}{\partial\eta_k\partial\eta_l}
        =\frac{c}{2}(\delta_i^k\delta_j^l+\delta_i^l\delta_j^k)
    \end{equation*}
    for all~$i,j,k,l$.
<!-- end definition-5 -->
<!-- note-2: body_md -->
\label{not:SimpleQuadratic}
    The variance function~$V$ is simple quadratic
    if and only if all the coefficients~$V_{ij}$
    are polynomials of degree at most two,
    whose quadratic part is~$c\eta_i\eta_j$.
<!-- end note-2 -->
<!-- remark-1: body_md -->
The variance function defined above coincides 
    with the variance function of a natural exponential family 
    (NEF) when the Hessian domain is determined by an NEF.
    In this case, the notion of ``simple quadratic'' 
    coincides with that in~\cite{Cas96}.
<!-- end remark-1 -->
<!-- lemma-1: body_md -->
\label{lem:CurvatureVariance}
    Let~$(U,\nabla,g=\nabla^2\psi)$ be a convex Hessian domain.
    Then, for the Hessian curvature tensor~$Q$
    and the variance function~$V$,
    the following holds:
    for all~$i,a,j,b$,
    \begin{equation*}
        Q_{iajb}=\frac12 g_{ak}g_{bl}
        \left(\frac{\partial^2V_{ij}}{\partial\eta_k\partial\eta_l}\circ(\nabla\psi)
        \right).
    \end{equation*}
    Here, we set~$Q_{iajb}=g\left(\frac{\partial }{\partial \theta^i},
        Q\left(\frac{\partial }{\partial \theta^a},\frac{\partial }{\partial \theta^j},
        \frac{\partial }{\partial \theta^b}\right)\right)$.
<!-- end lemma-1 -->
<!-- proof-1: body_md -->
We denote by~$(g^{ij})$the inverse matrix of~$(g_{ij})$.
    Since~$\frac{\partial \eta_a}{\partial \theta^b}=\psi_{ab}=g_{ab}$,
    we have~$\frac{\partial \theta^a}{\partial \eta_b}=g^{ab}$.
    Thus,
    \begin{align*}
        &\frac12 g_{ak}g_{bl}
        \left(\frac{\partial^2V_{ij}}{\partial\eta_k\partial\eta_l}\circ(\nabla\psi)
        \right)\\
        &=\frac12 g_{ak}g_{bl}\frac{\partial \theta^p}{\partial \eta_k}\frac{\partial }{\partial \theta^p}
        \left(\frac{\partial \theta^q}{\partial \eta_l}\frac{\partial }{\partial \theta^q}\psi_{ij}
        \right)
        =\frac12 g_{bl}
        \left(\frac{\partial g^{ql}}{\partial \theta^a}\psi_{ijq}
        +g^{ql}\psi_{ijaq}
        \right)\\
        &=-\frac12\frac{\partial g_{bl}}{\partial \theta^a}g^{ql}\psi_{ijq}
        +\frac12\psi_{ijab}
        =\frac12\psi_{ijab}-\frac12g^{ql}\psi_{ijq}\psi_{abl}
        =Q_{iajb}.
    \end{align*}
<!-- end proof-1 -->
<!-- proposition-3: body_md -->
\label{prop:CurvatureVariance}
    A Hessian domain~$(U,\nabla, g=\nabla^2\psi)$ has 
    constant Hessian sectional curvature~$c\in\mathbb{R}^{}$,
    if and only if its variance function~$V$ is simple quadratic.
<!-- end proposition-3 -->
<!-- proof-2: body_md -->
Since the argument is local, 
    we may assume that~$U$ is convex, 
    and the result follows immediately from Lemma~\ref{lem:CurvatureVariance}.
<!-- end proof-2 -->
<!-- proposition-4: body_md -->
\label{prop:OneMoreDimension}
    Let~$(U,\nabla, g=\nabla^2\psi)$ be a
    Hessian domain with constant Hessian sectional curvature
    $c\in\mathbb{R}^{}$.\\
    Then, the domain~$\tilde{U}:=\begin{cases}
        U\times \mathbb{R}^{}& (c< 0)\\
        U\times \mathbb{R}^{}& (c=0)\\
        \{(\theta,t)\subset U\times \mathbb{R}^{}~:~
        e^{-c\psi}-e^{t}>0\}&(c>0)
    \end{cases}$
    together with the function
    $\tilde{\psi}:=\begin{cases}
        \frac{1}{-c}\log(e^{-c\psi}+e^{t}) & (c< 0)\\
            \psi+e^{t}&(c=0)\\
            \frac{1}{-c}\log(e^{-c\psi}-e^{t}) & (c> 0)
        \end{cases}$
    defines another
    Hessian domain 
    $(\tilde{U}, \tilde{\nabla}, \tilde{g}:=\tilde{\nabla}^2\tilde{\psi})$
    with constant Hessian sectional curvature~$c$,
    where~$\tilde{\nabla}$ denotes the standard flat connection on~$\mathbb{R}^{n+1}$.
<!-- end proposition-4 -->
<!-- proof-3: body_md -->
The case~$c=0$ is trivial, since the resulting Hessian domain
    is simply a direct product of two Hessian domains
    $(U,\nabla, g)$ and~$(\mathbb{R}^{}, \nabla, e^t dt^2)$ 
    both of which
    have constant Hessian sectional curvature~$0$
    by assumption and  by direct computation, respectively. 

    We therefore assume~$c\neq 0$.
    Let~$s:=\mathrm{sgn}~c=\frac{c}{|c|}$.
    First, we show that
    $(\tilde{U}, \tilde{\nabla},\tilde{g}=\tilde{\nabla}^2\tilde{\psi})$
    is a Hessian domain.
    It suffices to show that
    $\tilde{g}$ is positive definite.
    With respect to the standard chart
    $(\theta^1,\ldots,\theta^n, t)$ on~$\mathbb{R}^{n+1}$,
    the Hessian matrix of~$\tilde{\psi}$
    is given by
    \begin{align*}
        (\tilde{\nabla}^2\tilde{\psi})_{ij}
        &=\begin{pmatrix}
            \frac{\psi_{ij}}{1-se^{t+c\psi}}
            +\frac{|c| e^{t+c\psi}\psi_i\psi_j}{(1-se^{t+c\psi})^2}&
            \frac{se^{t+c\psi}\psi_i}{(1-se^{t+c\psi})^2}\\
            \frac{se^{t+c\psi}\psi_j}{(1-se^{t+c\psi})^2}&
            \frac{e^{t+c\psi}}{|c|(1-se^{t+c\psi})^2}
        \end{pmatrix}\\
        &=\begin{pmatrix}
            \delta_i^a & c\psi_i\\
            0 &1
        \end{pmatrix}
        \begin{pmatrix}
            \frac{\psi_{ab}}{1-se^{t+c\psi}}
            & 0\\
            0 &
            \frac{e^{t+c\psi}}{|c|(1-se^{t+c\psi})^2}
        \end{pmatrix}
        \begin{pmatrix}
            \delta_j^b & 0\\
            c\psi_j &1
        \end{pmatrix}.
    \end{align*}
    Thus,~$\tilde{g}$ is positive definite.
    
    Next, we show the resulting Hessian domain~$\tilde{U}$ has
    constant Hessian sectional curvature~$c$.
    Since the argument is local, 
    we may assume that~$U$ and~$\tilde{U}$ are convex.
    With respect to the dual chart
    $(\tilde{\eta}_1,\ldots,\tilde{\eta}_n,\tilde{\eta}_t):=
    \left(\frac{\partial \tilde{\psi}}{\partial \theta^1},\ldots,
    \frac{\partial \tilde{\psi}}{\partial \theta^n},\frac{\partial \tilde{\psi}}{\partial t}\right)$
    of~$(\theta^1,\ldots,\theta^n,t)$,
    we have
    \begin{equation*}
        \tilde{\eta}_i=\frac{\psi_i}{1-se^{t+c\psi}},
        \quad \tilde{\eta}_t=\frac{e^{t+c\psi}}{|c|(1-se^{t+c\psi})}
    \end{equation*}
    and therefore~$\eta_i=\frac{\tilde{\eta}_i}{1+c\tilde{\eta}_t}$.
    Thus,
    the variance functions~$V, \tilde{V}$ of~$\psi, \tilde{\psi}$,
    respectively, satisfy
    \begin{align*}
        \tilde{V}(\tilde{\eta})
        &=\begin{pmatrix}
            \frac{\psi_{ij}}{1-se^{t+c\psi}}
            +\frac{|c| e^{t+c\psi}\psi_i\psi_j}{(1-se^{t+c\psi})^2}&
            \frac{se^{t+c\psi}\psi_i}{(1-se^{t+c\psi})^2}\\
            \frac{se^{t+c\psi}\psi_j}{(1-se^{t+c\psi})^2}&
            \frac{e^{t+c\psi}}{|c|(1-se^{t+c\psi})^2}
        \end{pmatrix}\\
        &=c\begin{pmatrix}
            \tilde{\eta}_i\tilde{\eta}_j 
            &\tilde{\eta}_i\tilde{\eta}_t\\
            \tilde{\eta}_j\tilde{\eta}_t
            &\tilde{\eta}_t^2
        \end{pmatrix}
        +\begin{pmatrix}
            (1+c\tilde{\eta}_t)(V_{ij}(\eta)-c\eta_i\eta_j)
            &0\\
            0& \tilde{\eta}_t
        \end{pmatrix}.
    \end{align*}
    It follows from Note~\ref{not:SimpleQuadratic} that
    they are simple quadratic. 
    The claim follows from Proposition~\ref{prop:CurvatureVariance}.
<!-- end proof-3 -->
<!-- remark-2: body_md -->
When~$c\leq0$, we have~$\{(\theta,t)\subset U\times \mathbb{R}^{}~:~
    e^{-c\psi}-se^{t}>0\}=U\times \mathbb{R}^{}$.
    Moreover, the limit of~$\frac{1}{-c}\log(e^{-c\psi}-se^{t}) $
    as~$c\rightarrow 0$
    coincides with~$\psi+e^{t}$.
<!-- end remark-2 -->
<!-- proposition-5: body_md -->
\label{prop:BeingStandardModels}
    Let~$c\in \mathbb{R}^{}$. \\
    All the standard models
    $\begin{cases}
        \mathcal{S}^n(c) & (c<0)\\
        \mathcal{R}^{n,k}(c)~(k=0,\ldots, n)& (c=0)\\
        \mathcal{H}^n(c), \mathcal{H}^{n,\mathrm{H}}(c),
    \mathcal{H}^{n,k}(c)~(k=1\ldots, n) & (c>0)
    \end{cases}$
    defined in 
    Example~\ref{exm:StandardModels}
    have constant Hessian sectional curvature~$c$.
<!-- end proposition-5 -->
<!-- proof-4: body_md -->
When~$c<0$,
    $\mathcal{S}^1(c)$ has constant Hessian sectional curvature
    $c$ by direct computation.
    Then, by repeatedly applying Proposition~\ref{prop:OneMoreDimension},
    the claim follows for any~$n$.

    When~$c=0$,
    for any~$k\in\mathbb{Z}_{\geq 0}$,
    $\mathcal{R}^{k,k}(0)$ has
    constant Hessian sectional curvature~$0$
    by direct computation.
    Then, by repeatedly applying Proposition~\ref{prop:OneMoreDimension},
    the claim follows for any~$n$ and~$k=0,\ldots, n$.

    When~$c<0$, for any~$n$,
    $\mathcal{H}^{n}(c)$ and~$\mathcal{H}^{n,\mathrm{H}}(c)$
    has constant Hessian sectional curvature~$c$ by direct computation.
    Moreover, for any~$n$,
    it was proved in \cite[Theorem 7]{Shi95}
    that 
    $\mathcal{H}^{n,n}(c)$ has constant Hessian sectional curvature
    $c$.
    Thus, by repeatedly applying Proposition~\ref{prop:OneMoreDimension},
    the claim follows.
<!-- end proof-4 -->
<!-- definition-6: body_md -->
\label{def:Maximality}
    (1)~For a pair~$(U,f)$ consisting of
    a domain~$U\subset \mathbb{R}^{n}$ and an analytic function~$f\colon U\rightarrow\mathbb{R}^{}$,
    we define an order relation~$\leq$ by
    \begin{equation*}
        (U,f)\leq (U',f')\overset{\mathrm{def}}{\Leftrightarrow}
        U\subset U'~\mathrm{and}~f'|_U=f.
    \end{equation*}
    (2)~For a pair~$(U,g)$ consisting of
    a domain~$U\subset \mathbb{R}^{n}$ and an analytic Riemannian metric~$g$ on~$U$,
    we define an order relation~$\leq$ by
    \begin{equation*}
        (U,g)\leq (U',g')\overset{\mathrm{def}}{\Leftrightarrow}
        U\subset U'~\mathrm{and}~g'|_U=g.
    \end{equation*}
<!-- end definition-6 -->
<!-- note-3: body_md -->
\label{not:DomainSum}
    Let~$U,U'$ be domains and~$f, f'$ be analytic 
    functions on~$U,U'$, respectively.
    Suppose that~$U\cap U'$ is connected and 
    that~$f=f'$ on~$U\cap U'$.
    Then,~$U\cup U'$ is a domain, that is a connected open subset
    of~$\mathbb{R}^{n}$,
    and
    $(U,f), (U', f') \leq (U\cup U', \tilde{f})$
    where
    $\tilde{f}\colon U\cup U'\rightarrow\mathbb{R}^{}$
    is defined by
    $\tilde{f}:=f$ on~$U$ and~$\tilde{f}:=f'$ on~$U'$.
<!-- end note-3 -->
<!-- note-4: body_md -->
\label{not:PotentialAnaliticity}
    For a Hessian domain~$(U,\nabla, g)$
    whose Riemannian metric~$g$ is analytic, 
    there exists locally an analytic Hessian potential
    of~$g$, by applying the real analytic version of the Poincar\'{e} lemma
    to the argument in \cite[Proposition 2.1]{Shi07}.
<!-- end note-4 -->
<!-- lemma-2: body_md -->
\label{lem:Maximalities}
    For a convex Hessian domain~$(U,\nabla, g=\nabla^2\psi)$
    whose Riemannian metric~$g$ and Hessian potential~$\psi$
    are analytic,
    if~$(U,\psi)$ is maximal,
    then~$(U,g)$ is also maximal.
<!-- end lemma-2 -->
<!-- proof-5: body_md -->
Suppose that a pair~$(U', g')$ of
    a domain~$U'\subset \mathbb{R}^{n}$
    and an analytic Riemannian metric~$g'$ on~$U'$,
    satisfies~$(U,\nabla^2\psi)\leq (U', g')$.
    We may assume that~$(\nabla, g')$
    defines a Hessian structure on~$U'$
    by Fact~\ref{fac:HessianCondition}.
    It suffices to show that~$U$ is 
    a closed subset of~$U'$,
    equivalently, that~$\overline{U}\cap U'=U$.
    The inclusion~$U\subset \overline{U}\cap U'$ is clear.
    It remains to show that~$\overline{U}\cap U'\subset U$.
    Let~$p\in \overline{U}\cap U'$,
    and let
    $V\subset \mathbb{R}^{n}$ be an open convex neighborhood of~$p$ with~$V\subset U'$,
    such that an analytic Hessian potential~$\psi'$ of~$g'$
    exists on~$V$.
    Then~$U\cap V$ is convex, and since
    $\nabla^2\psi=g=g'=\nabla^2\psi'$,
    we may assume~$\psi'=\psi$ on~$U\cap V$.
    Hence, by Note~\ref{not:DomainSum},
    $\psi$ extends to~$U\cup V$.
    By maximality, we have~$U\cup V=U$,
    and in particular~$p\in U$.
<!-- end proof-5 -->
<!-- lemma-3: body_md -->
\label{lem:LogMaximality}
    Let~$f\colon \mathbb{R}^{n}\rightarrow\mathbb{R}^{}$ be an analytic function
    and~$U$ be one of the connected components of~$f^{-1}(\mathbb{R}^{}_{>0})$.
    Then,~$(U,\log f)$ is maximal.
<!-- end lemma-3 -->
<!-- proof-6: body_md -->
Suppose that a pair~$(U', f')$ of
    a domain~$U'\subset \mathbb{R}^{n}$
    and an analytic function~$f'$ on~$U'$,
    satisfies~$(U,\log f)\leq (U',f')$.
    Then~$f=e^{f'}>0$ on~$U$,
    and hence, by analiticity, also on~$U'$.
    Thus~$U'\subset f^{-1}(\mathbb{R}^{}_{>0})$
    and
    $(U', f')=(U,\log f)$.
<!-- end proof-6 -->
<!-- proposition-6: body_md -->
\label{prop:MaximalityOfModels}
    The standard models (Example~\ref{exm:StandardModels})
    are convex and maximal.
<!-- end proposition-6 -->
<!-- proof-7: body_md -->
Let~$(U,\nabla,g=\nabla^2\psi)$ denote
    one of the standard models.
    Since~$U$ is a level set of a convex function,
    $U\subset \mathbb{R}^{n}$ is convex.
    Moreover, by Lemma~\ref{lem:LogMaximality},
    $(U, \psi)$ is maximal,
    and hence,
    by Lemma~\ref{lem:Maximalities},
    $(U,\nabla^2\psi)$ is maximal.
<!-- end proof-7 -->
<!-- definition-7: body_md -->
Let~$M$ and~$M'$ be manifolds equipped with affine connections
    $\nabla$ and~$\nabla'$, respectively.
    A local diffeomorphism~$f\colon M\rightarrow M'$ is said to be
     \textit{connection-preserving}
    if it satisfies~$f_*(\nabla_XY)=\nabla'_{f_*X}(f_*Y)$
    for any locally defined vector fields~$X$ and~$Y$ on~$M$.
<!-- end definition-7 -->
<!-- definition-8: body_md -->
Let~$(M,\nabla,g)$ and~$(M',\nabla',g')$
    be Hessian manifolds.
    A local diffeomorphism~$f\colon M\rightarrow M'$ is said to 
    \textit{preserve the
    Hessian structure} if
    it is a connection-preserving isometry.
<!-- end definition-8 -->
<!-- fact-3: body_md -->
\label{fac:AffineExtension}
    Let~$\nabla, \nabla'$ be analytic affine connections
    on analytic manifolds~$M, M'$, respectively.
    Suppose that~$M$ is connected and simply connected,
    and that~$\nabla'$ is complete.
    Then, for any connected open subset~$V\subset M$,
    every connection-preserving local diffeomorphism
    $f\colon V\rightarrow M'$
    uniquely extends to a 
    connection-preserving local diffeomorphism~$\tilde{f}\colon M\rightarrow M'$.
<!-- end fact-3 -->
<!-- proposition-7: body_md -->
\label{prop:HessianExtension}
    Let~$(M,\nabla',g')$ be
    an~$n$-dimensional connected and simply connected Hessian manifold,
    and let~$(U,\nabla, g=\nabla^2\psi)$
    be an~$n$-dimensional convex maximal Hessian domain.
    Suppose that the manifold~$M$, 
    the affine connections~$\nabla', \nabla$,
    the Riemannian metric~$g', g$,
    and the Hessian potential~$\psi$ are all analytic.
    Then, for any connected open subset~$V\subset M$,
    every local diffeomorphism
    $f\colon V\rightarrow U$ preserving the Hessian structures
    uniquely extends to a 
    local isomorphism~$\tilde{f}\colon M\rightarrow U$
    preserving the Hessian structures.
<!-- end proposition-7 -->
<!-- proof-8: body_md -->
By Fact~\ref{fac:AffineExtension} and 
    analiticity,
    $f$ extends to a connection-preserving
    local diffeomorphism~$\tilde{f}\colon M\rightarrow \mathbb{R}^{n}.$
    Then,~$\tilde{f}(M)\subset \mathbb{R}^{n}$ is a connected open subset.

    It suffices to show that~$\tilde{f}(M)\cap \overline{U}\subset U$.
    Indeed, since
    $\tilde{f}(M)=(\tilde{f}(M)\cap\overline{U})\sqcup
    (\tilde{f}(M)\cap \mathbb{R}^{n}\setminus\overline{U})
    \subset (\tilde{f}(M)\cap U)\sqcup
    (\tilde{f}(M)\cap \mathbb{R}^{n}\setminus\overline{U})$,
    and since~$\tilde{f}(M)\cap U\neq \emptyset$
    and~$\tilde{f}(M)$ is connected,
    it follows that~$\tilde{f}(M)\subset U$.
    
    We show that~$\tilde{f}(M)\cap \overline{U}\subset U$.
    Let~$p\in\tilde{f}(M)\cap \overline{U}$, and
    suppose that for a convex open neighborhood~$V\subset \tilde{f}(M)$
    of~$p$
    and an open subset~$W\subset M$,
    $f|_W: W\rightarrow V$ is a diffeomorphism.
    Then the Riemannian metric~$g'':=(f|_W^{-1})^*g'$
    on~$V$ satisfies~$g''=(f|_W^{-1})^*g'=(f|_W^{-1})^*f^*g=g$
    on~$V\cap U$.
    Thus,~$g$ extends to~$U\cup V$, 
    and hence~$U\cup V\subset U$ by the maximality of~$U$.
    In particular,~$p\in U$.
<!-- end proof-8 -->
<!-- corollary-1: body_md -->
\label{cor:ConvexMaximalIsomorphism}
    Let~$(U,\nabla, g=\nabla^2\psi),~(U',\nabla', g'=(\nabla')^2\psi')$ be
    $n$-dimensional convex maximal Hessian domains
    whose Riemannian metrics are analytic.
    Then, for any connected open subset~$V\subset U$,
    every local diffeomorphism
    $f\colon V\rightarrow U'$ preserving the Hessian structures
    uniquely extends to a 
    diffeomorphism~$\tilde{f}\colon U\rightarrow U'$
    preserving Hessian structures.
<!-- end corollary-1 -->
<!-- proof-9: body_md -->
By Proposition~\ref{prop:HessianExtension},
    $f$ extends to a local isomorphism~$\tilde{f}\colon U\rightarrow U'$
    preserving the Hessian structures.
    Since~$U$ is convex, it follows that~$\tilde{f}$ is injective.
    Thus,~$\tilde{f}(U)\subset U'\subset \mathbb{R}^{n}$
    is a convex maximal Hessian domain,
    and hence~$\tilde{f}(U)= U'$ by the maximality of~$U'$.
<!-- end proof-9 -->
<!-- proposition-8: body_md -->
\label{prop:LocalHessianEmbedding}
    Let~$M$ be a Hessian manifold with 
    constant Hessian sectional curvature~$c\in\mathbb{R}^{}$.
    Then, there exists 
    an open subset~$U\subset M$ and
    one of the standard models~$\tilde{M}$
    with constant Hessian sectional curvature~$c\in \mathbb{R}^{}$,
    such that
    there is a local diffeomorphism~$f\colon U\rightarrow \tilde{M}$
    preserving the Hessian structures.
<!-- end proposition-8 -->
<!-- lemma-4: body_md -->
\label{lem:CHCAnalyticity}
    A Hessian manifold~$(M,\nabla, g)$ with 
    constant Hessian sectional curvature~$c\in\mathbb{R}^{}$
    admits an real-analytic structure for which
    the affine connection and the Riemannian metric are analytic.
<!-- end lemma-4 -->
<!-- proof-10: body_md -->
Since the argument is local, 
    we may assume that~$M$ is a Hessian domain.
    By Fact~\ref{fac:TangentBundleKahler},
    the tangent bundle~$M\times \mathbb{R}^{n}$ carries a
    K\"{a}hler~structure.
    Then, by Fact~\ref{fac:TangentCurvature},
    $M\times \mathbb{R}^{n}$ has constant holomorphic sectional curvature
    (see \cite{KN69} for the definition).
    Hence, by Fact~\ref{fac:ComplexSpaceFormsEmbedding},
    $M\times \mathbb{R}^{n}$ admits a real-analytic structure with respect to 
    which
    all the tensors of the K\"{a}hler~structure are real-analytic.
    Since, by Note~\ref{not:TangentHolomorphicChart},
    the map~$M\times \mathbb{R}^{n}\rightarrow M+\sqrt{-1} \mathbb{R}^{n},~(p,v)\mapsto
    p+\sqrt{-1} v$ defines a complex chart,
    we may regard~$M$ as an analytic submanifold of~$M\times \mathbb{R}^{n}$
    via the embedding~$M\rightarrow M\times \mathbb{R}^{n},~p\mapsto (p, 0)$.
    Thus, the standard chart on~$M$ is real-analytic with
    respect to the induced analytic structure on~$M$,
    and therefore the affine connection~$\nabla$ is
    real-analytic.
    Moreover, again by Fact~\ref{fac:TangentBundleKahler},
    the Riemannian metric~$g$ is 
    real-analytic with
    respect to the induced analytic structure on~$M$.
<!-- end proof-10 -->
<!-- proof-11: body_md -->
The local diffeomorphism obtained in Proposition~\ref{prop:LocalHessianEmbedding}
    is real-analytic with respect to the analytic structure
    given by Lemma~\ref{lem:CHCAnalyticity}.
    Thus, by Proposition~\ref{prop:HessianExtension},
    it extends to a globally defined local diffeomorphism.
<!-- end proof-11 -->
<!-- definition-9: body_md -->
(1)~A~$(1,1)$-tensor field~$I$ on~$N$ is called
    an \textit{almost complex structure} if it satisfies
    $I^2=-\mathrm{id}$.\\
    (2)~An almost complex structure~$I$ on~$N$
    is said to be \textit{integrable}
    if, for every point of~$N$,
    there exists a chart around the point with respect to which 
    the matrix representation of~$I$
    is given by~$\begin{pmatrix}
        0&-1_n\\ 1_n &0
    \end{pmatrix}$.
    In this case,~$I$ is called a \textit{complex structure},
    and such a chart is called a \textit{complex chart}.
<!-- end definition-9 -->
<!-- note-5: body_md -->
The complex Euclidean space~$\mathbb{C}^{n}$
    is identified with~$\mathbb{R}^{2n}$
    via the map
    $(z^1,\ldots, z^n)\mapsto (x^1,\ldots, x^n, y^1,\ldots, y^n)
    :=(\Re z^1,\ldots, \Re z^n,\Im z^1,\ldots, \Im z^n)$.
    Then, defining an almost complex structure~$I$
    by~$I:=\begin{pmatrix}
        0&-1_n\\ 1_n &0
    \end{pmatrix}$
    with respect to the chart
    $(x^1,\ldots, x^n, y^1,\ldots, y^n)$,
    $I$ is an integrable complex structure on~$\mathbb{C}^{n}$,
    called the standard complex structure on~$\mathbb{C}^{n}$.
<!-- end note-5 -->
<!-- fact-4: body_md -->
\label{fac:Nijenhuis}
    The integrability of an almost complex structure
    can be characterized by the \textit{Nijenhuis tensor}, which is 
    defined for any~$(1,1)$-tensor field~$A$ by
    \begin{equation*}
        N_A(X,Y):=A^2[X,Y]-A([AX,Y]+[X,AY])+[AX,AY].
    \end{equation*}
    An almost complex structure is integrable
    if and only if its Nijenhuis tensor vanishes (the
    Newlander-Nirenberg theorem).
<!-- end fact-4 -->
<!-- definition-10: body_md -->
For a complex structure~$I$, a Riemannian metric~$h$,
    and a symplectic structure~$\omega$ on~$N$,
    $(I,h,\omega)$ is called a \textit{K\"{a}hler~structure}
    on~$N$
    if it satisfies the following identity:
    \begin{equation*}
        \omega(\cdot, \cdot)=h(I\cdot, \cdot).
    \end{equation*}
<!-- end definition-10 -->
<!-- lemma-5: body_md -->
\label{lem:KahlerCompatibility}
    A K\"{a}hler~structure~$(I,h,\omega)$ on~$N$
    satisfies the following identities:
    \begin{equation*}
        h(I\cdot, I\cdot)=h(\cdot, \cdot), 
        \quad
        \omega(I\cdot, I\cdot)=\omega(\cdot, \cdot).
    \end{equation*}
<!-- end lemma-5 -->
<!-- proof-12: body_md -->
The claim follows immediately from the definition.
<!-- end proof-12 -->
<!-- fact-5: body_md -->
\label{fac:KahlerPotential}
    (1)~Let~$\Psi\colon U\rightarrow \mathbb{R}^{}$
    be a smooth function on
    an open subset~$U\subset \mathbb{C}^{n}$
    such that the Hermitian matrix
    $\left(
        \frac{\partial^2\Psi}{\partial z^i \partial \bar{z}^j}
    \right)$
    is positive definite at every point.
    Let~$I$ be the standard complex structure,
    and define
    \begin{equation}\label{eq:KahlerPotential}
        \begin{aligned}
            h&:=\frac{\partial^2\Psi}{\partial z^i \partial \bar{z}^j}
            (dz^i\otimes d\bar{z}^j+d\bar{z}^j\otimes dz^i)\\
            \omega&:=\sqrt{-1}
            \frac{\partial^2\Psi}{\partial z^i \partial \bar{z}^j}
            (dz^i\otimes d\bar{z}^j-d\bar{z}^j\otimes dz^i).
        \end{aligned}
    \end{equation}
    Then~$(I,h,\omega)$ is a K\"{a}hler~structure on~$U$.\\
    (2)~Let~$(N, I,h,\omega)$ be a K\"{a}hler~manifold.
    For any~$p\in N$, there exist an open neighborhood
    $U\subset N$, a complex chart~$(z^1,\ldots, z^n)$,
    and a smooth function~$\Psi\colon U\rightarrow \mathbb{R}^{}$
    such that~$\Psi$ satisfies equation (\ref{eq:KahlerPotential}).
    In this case,~$\Psi$ is called a \textit{K\"{a}hler~potential}.
<!-- end fact-5 -->
<!-- note-6: body_md -->
\label{not:KahlerPotentialDifference}
    Suppose that smooth functions~$\Psi, \Psi'\colon U\rightarrow \mathbb{R}^{}$
    on an open subset~$U\subset \mathbb{C}^{n}$
    satisfy the condition in Fact~\ref{fac:KahlerPotential} (1).
    If~$\Psi'-\Psi=\Re F$ for some holomorphic function
    $F\colon U\rightarrow \mathbb{C}^{n}$,
    then~$\Psi$ and~$\Psi'$ gives the same 
    K\"{a}hler~structure~$(I,h,\omega)$ on~$U$.
<!-- end note-6 -->
<!-- definition-11: body_md -->
\label{def:Hamiltonian}
    The action of a Lie group~$G$ on a
    symplectic manifold~$(N,\omega)$ is said to be a
    \textit{Hamiltonian action}
    if it preserves~$\omega$
    and there exists a map~$\mu\colon N\rightarrow
    \mathfrak{g}^*$ satisfying the following conditions:\\
    (i)~For any~$X\in\mathfrak{g}$,~$d\langle \mu, X\rangle=\omega(X^V,\cdot).$\\
    (ii)~For any~$g\in G$,~$Ad_{g}^*:=(Ad_{g^{-1}})^*$ satisfies
    $Ad_{g}^*\circ\mu=\mu\circ g$.\\
    In this case,~$\mu$ is called a \textit{moment map}.
    Here,~$X^V$ denotes the vector field on~$N$ generated by~$X\in\mathfrak{g}$.
<!-- end definition-11 -->
<!-- definition-12: body_md -->
In this paper, 
    a Hamiltonian action on a K\"{a}hler~manifold
    means an action that preserves the K\"{a}hler~structure 
    and is Hamiltonian as an action on the underlying symplectic manifold.
<!-- end definition-12 -->
<!-- note-7: body_md -->
\label{not:AbelianHamiltonianAction}
    In particular, 
    when~$G$ is abelian, 
    the adjoint representation is trivial, 
    that is,~$Ad_g=\mathrm{id}$ for any~$g\in G$. 
    Hence, condition (ii) is equivalent to~$\mu$ being~$G$-invariant.

    Moreover, condition (i) implies that the subspace generated 
    by~$\mathfrak{g}$ at each point is isotropic. 
    Namely,~$\omega(X^V,Y^V)=0$ for any~$X,Y\in\mathfrak{g}$.
<!-- end note-7 -->
<!-- proposition-9: body_md -->
\label{prop:MomentMaps}
    Let~$\omega, \omega'$ be symplectic structures on
    manifolds~$N, N'$, respectively, 
    and let 
    Lie groups~$G, G'$ act on~$N, N'$
    preserving the symplectic structures, respectively.
    Suppose that
    a local diffeomorphism~$F\colon N'\rightarrow N$
    preserving the symplectic structures 
    and a surjective Lie group 
    homomorphism
    $\rho\colon G'\rightarrow G$ satisfy the following condition:\\
    (i)~For any~$ p\in N'$ and~$g\in G',~ F(g\cdot p)=\rho(g)\cdot F(p).$\\
    Moreover, smooth maps~$\mu\colon N\rightarrow \mathfrak{g}^*$
    and ~$\mu'\colon N'\rightarrow (\mathfrak{g}')^*$
    satisfy the following condition:\\
    (ii)~$\mu'=\rho^*\circ\mu\circ F.$\\
    Then, if~$\mu'$ is a moment map, then~$\mu$ is also a moment map.
<!-- end proposition-9 -->
<!-- proof-13: body_md -->
It follows by a straightforward argument.
<!-- end proof-13 -->
<!-- fact-6: body_md -->
\label{fac:TangentBundleKahler}
    It is known that the tangent bundle of 
    a Hessian manifold naturally 
    admits a K\"{a}hler~structure (see \cite{Shi07} for details).
    In particular, for a Hessian domain~$(U,\nabla,g=\nabla^2\psi)$, 
    the K\"{a}hler~structure~$(I,h,\omega)$ on~$TU\cong U\times \mathbb{R}^{n}$ 
    is given by:
    For any~$X, Y\in \mathbb{R}^{n}$,
    \begin{equation}\label{eq:TangentKahlerStructure}
        \begin{alignedat}{2}
        &IX^H:=X^V, \quad&
        &IX^V:=-X^H\\
        &h(X^H,Y^H)
        =h(X^V,Y^V)
        :=g(X^B, Y^B)\circ\mathrm{pr}_1, \quad&
        &h(X^H,Y^V)
        =h(X^V,Y^H):=0,\\
        &\omega(X^H,Y^V)
        =-\omega(X^V,Y^H)
        :=g(X^B, Y^B)\circ\mathrm{pr}_1, \quad&
        &\omega(X^H,Y^H)
        =\omega(X^V,Y^V):=0.
    \end{alignedat}
    \end{equation}
    Here,~$\mathrm{pr}_1\colon U\times \mathbb{R}^{n}\rightarrow U$ 
    and~$\mathrm{pr}_2\colon U\times \mathbb{R}^{n}\rightarrow \mathbb{R}^{n}$ denote 
    the projections onto the respective factors.
    For~$X\in\mathbb{R}^{n}$, 
    regarding~$X$ as a vector field on~$U$, we define~$X^H:=\mathrm{pr}_1^*X$.
    Similarly, regarding~$X$ as a vector field on the vector space~$\mathbb{R}^{n}$, 
    we define~$X^V:=\mathrm{pr}_2^*X$.
    Then,~$\Psi:=4(\psi\circ\mathrm{pr}_1)$ 
    is a K\"{a}hler~potential for the natural K\"{a}hler~structure.
<!-- end fact-6 -->
<!-- proposition-10: body_md -->
\label{prop:TangentMomentMap}
    The action of~$\mathbb{R}^{n}$ 
    on the tangent bundle~$TU\cong U\times \mathbb{R}^{n}$ 
    by translations in the second factor is an effective, proper, 
    free and Hamiltonian action preserving the K\"{a}hler~structure.
    Moreover, define
    \begin{equation*}
        \nu\colon U\rightarrow (\mathbb{R}^{n})^*,~
        p\mapsto (X\mapsto -d\psi_p(X)).
    \end{equation*}
    Then~$\mu:=\nu\circ\mathrm{pr}_1\colon U\times \mathbb{R}^{n}\rightarrow (\mathbb{R}^{n})^*$
    is a moment map.
    In particular, the~$\mathbb{R}^{n}$-action generates an isotropic subspace
    at every point on~$U\times \mathbb{R}^{n}$.
<!-- end proposition-10 -->
<!-- proof-14: body_md -->
The~$\mathbb{R}^{n}$-action is clearly effective, proper, and free.
    By Fact~\ref{fac:TangentBundleKahler}, 
    the~$\mathbb{R}^{n}$-action preserves~$X^H$ and~$X^V$ 
    for any~$X\in\mathbb{R}^{n}$, and hence preserves the K\"{a}hler~structure.
    Next, for~$\mu$, for any~$X,Y\in\mathbb{R}^{n}$, we have
    \begin{align*}
        d\langle\mu, X\rangle(Y^H)&=d(\langle\nu,X\rangle\circ\mathrm{pr}_1)(Y^H)
        =-d((X\psi)\circ\mathrm{pr}_1)(Y^H)\\
        &=-(XY\psi)\circ\mathrm{pr}_1=-g(X,Y)\circ\mathrm{pr}_1=\omega(X^V, Y^H),\\
        d\langle\mu, X\rangle(Y^V)&=d(\langle\nu,X\rangle\circ\mathrm{pr}_1)(Y^V)=0
        =\omega(X^V, Y^V).
    \end{align*}
    Thus,~$\mu$ is a moment map.
    Finally, by Note~\ref{not:AbelianHamiltonianAction}, 
    the~$\mathbb{R}^{n}$-action generates an isotropic subspace 
    at every point on~$U\times \mathbb{R}^{n}$.
<!-- end proof-14 -->
<!-- remark-3: body_md -->
As described in Section~\ref{sec:QuotientHessian}, 
    for a Hessian domain~$U$, 
    the quotient manifold~$(U\times \mathbb{R}^{n})/\mathbb{R}^{n}$ 
    naturally admits a Hessian structure and 
    is isomorphic to~$U$ as a Hessian manifold 
    (Lemma~\ref{lem:TangentBundleQuotient}).
<!-- end remark-3 -->
<!-- fact-7: body_md -->
\label{fac:TangentCurvature}
    For a Hessian manifold~$M$ ans the tangent bundle~$TM$,
    the following conditions are equivalent:\\
    (a)~$M$ has constant Hessian sectional curvature~$c$.\\
    (b)~$TM$ has constant holomorphic sectional curvature~$-c$.
<!-- end fact-7 -->
<!-- note-8: body_md -->
\label{not:TangentHolomorphicChart}
    For a Hessian domain~$(U,\nabla,g)$,
    $U\times \mathbb{R}^{n}$ is naturally identified with~$U+\sqrt{-1}\mathbb{R}^{n}\subset \mathbb{C}^{n}$
    as complex manifolds via the map
    $U\times \mathbb{R}^{n}\rightarrow U+\sqrt{-1}\mathbb{R}^{n}\subset \mathbb{C}^{n},~ (p,v)\mapsto p+\sqrt{-1} v$.
    In particular,
    for the standard chart~$(\theta^1,\ldots,\theta^n)$ on~$U$
    and the standard chart~$(v^1,\ldots, v^n)$ on~$\mathbb{R}^{n}$,
    the functions~$(w^1,\ldots, w^n)$ defined by 
    $w^i:=\theta^i\circ\mathrm{pr}_1 +\sqrt{-1} v^i$
    form a global complex chart on~$U\times \mathbb{R}^{n}$.
<!-- end note-8 -->
<!-- example-2: body_md -->
\label{exm:StandardModelsKahler}
    On the tangent bundles of the standard models 
    (Example~\ref{exm:StandardModels}), 
    the K\"{a}hler~potential~$\Psi$ 
    defined in Fact~\ref{fac:TangentBundleKahler} 
    and the moment map~$\mu$ defined 
    in Proposition~\ref{prop:TangentMomentMap} 
    are given in the following form 
    with respect to the global complex chart
    $(w^1,\ldots,w^n)$ in Note~\ref{not:TangentHolomorphicChart}.

    (1)~Let~$c<0$. For~$\mathcal{S}^n(c)$,
    \begin{align*}
        \Psi&=-\frac{4}{c}\log\left(1+e^{\Re w^1}+\cdots+e^{\Re w^n}\right),\\
        \mu&=
        \frac{1}{c\left(1+e^{\Re w^1}+\cdots+e^{\Re w^n}\right)}
        \left(e^{\Re w^1}, \ldots, e^{\Re w^n}\right).
    \end{align*}
    (2)~Let~$k=0,\ldots, n$. For~$M:=\mathcal{R}^{n,k}(0)$,
    \begin{align*}
        \Psi&=2(\Re w^1)^2+\cdots+2(\Re w^k)^2+4e^{\Re w^{k+1}}
            +\cdots+4e^{\Re w^{n}},\\
        \mu&=-\left(\Re w^1,\ldots, \Re w^k,
        e^{\Re w^{k+1}},\ldots, e^{\Re w^n}\right).
    \end{align*}
    (3)~Let~$c>0$.\\
    (3-i)~For~$\mathcal{H}^n(c)$,
    \begin{align*}
        \Psi&=-\frac{4}{c}\log\left(1-e^{\Re w^1}-\cdots-e^{\Re w^n}\right),\\
        \mu&=\frac{1}{c\left(1-e^{\Re w^1}+\cdots-e^{\Re w^n}\right)}
        \left(e^{\Re w^1}, \ldots, e^{\Re w^n}\right).
    \end{align*}
    (3-ii)~For~$\mathcal{H}^{n,\mathrm{H}}(c)$,
    \begin{align*}
        \Psi&=-\frac{4}{c}\log\left(\cos {\Re w^1}-e^{\Re w^2}-\cdots-e^{\Re w^n}\right),\\
        \mu&=\frac{1}{c\left(\cos\Re w^1-e^{\Re w^2}-\cdots-e^{\Re w^n}\right)}
    \left(\sin \Re w^1, e^{\Re w^2},\ldots,e^{\Re w^2}\right).
    \end{align*}
    (3-iii)~Let~$k=1,\ldots, n$. For~$\mathcal{H}^{n,k}(c)$,
    \begin{align*}
        \Psi&=-\frac{4}{c}\log\left(-\Re w^1-\frac{1}{2}(\Re w^2)^2-\cdots
        -\frac{1}{2}(\Re w^k)^2
            -e^{\Re w^{k+1}}-\cdots-e^{\Re w^n}\right),\\
        \mu&=\frac{\left(1, \Re w^2,\ldots, \Re w^k,
    e^{\Re w^{k+1}},\ldots, e^{\Re w^n}\right)}{c\left(-\Re w^1-
    \frac{1}{2}(\Re w^2)^2-\cdots- \frac{1}{2}(\Re w^k)^2
    -e^{\Re w^{k+1}}-\cdots-e^{\Re w^n}\right)}.
    \end{align*}
<!-- end example-2 -->
<!-- definition-13: body_md -->
For~$X\in \mathfrak{a}$,
    we denote by~$X^V$ the vector field on~$N$ generated by~$X$,
    and define~$X^H:=-IX^V$.
    Moreover, we define
    \begin{equation*}
        N^\circ_\mathbb{A}:=\{p\in N~:~ \mathbb{A}_p=\{e\}\},
    \end{equation*}
    where~$\mathbb{A}_p$ denotes the isotropy subgroup of~$\mathbb{A}$
    at~$p\in N$.
<!-- end definition-13 -->
<!-- note-9: body_md -->
Since~$I$ is~$\mathbb{A}$-invariant,
    $X^H$ is also~$\mathbb{A}$-invariant.
<!-- end note-9 -->
<!-- lemma-6: body_md -->
\label{lem:LieBrackets}
    For any~$X, Y\in\mathfrak{a}$, we have
    \begin{equation*}
        [X^H, Y^H]=[X^V, Y^H]=[X^V, Y^V]=0.
    \end{equation*}
<!-- end lemma-6 -->
<!-- proof-15: body_md -->
Since~$\mathbb{A}$ is abelian, we have~$[X^V,Y^V]=0.$
    Since~$I$ is~$\mathbb{A}$-invariant,
    for any vector field~$A$ on~$N$,
    \begin{equation*}
        0=(\mathcal{L}_{X^V}I)A=[X^V, IA]-I[X^V, A].
    \end{equation*}
    In particular,
    \begin{equation*}
        [X^V, Y^H]=[X^V, -IY^V]=-I[X^V,Y^V]=0.
    \end{equation*}
    Moreover, by Fact~\ref{fac:Nijenhuis},
    the Nijenhuis tensor~$N_I$ of~$I$ vanishes.
    Thus,
    \begin{equation*}
        0=N_I(X^V, Y^V)
        =-[X^V,Y^V]-I([IX^V, Y^V]+[X^V, IY^V])+[IX^V, IY^V]
        =[X^H,Y^H].
    \end{equation*}
<!-- end proof-15 -->
<!-- lemma-7: body_md -->
\label{lem:Lagrangeness}
    (1)~For any~$X\in \mathfrak{a}$, we have
    \begin{equation*}
        IX^H= X^V,\quad IX^V=-X^H.
    \end{equation*}
    (2)~For any~$X, Y\in \mathfrak{a}$, we have
    \begin{alignat*}{2}
        &h(X^H,Y^H)=h(X^V,Y^V), \quad&
        &h(X^H,Y^V)=h(X^V,Y^H)=0,\\
        &\omega(X^H,Y^V)=-\omega(X^V,Y^H), \quad&
        &\omega(X^H,Y^H)=\omega(X^V,Y^V)=0.
    \end{alignat*}
    (3)~For any~$X,Y ,Z\in\mathfrak{a}$, we have
    \begin{equation*}
        X^Hh(Y^H,Z^H)=Y^Hh(X^H,Z^H).
    \end{equation*}
<!-- end lemma-7 -->
<!-- proof-16: body_md -->
(1) follows immediately from the definition.
    For~(2), 
    since the moment map~$\mu$ is~$\mathbb{A}$-invariant,
    for any~$X,Y\in\mathfrak{a}$,
    $0=d\langle\mu, X\rangle(Y)=\omega(X^V,Y^V)$.
    The rest follows from Lemma~\ref{lem:KahlerCompatibility}.

    For (3), since~$d\omega=0$, for any~$X,Y,Z\in\mathfrak{a}$,
    by Lemma~\ref{lem:LieBrackets},
    \begin{align*}
        0&=(d\omega)(X^H,Y^H,Z^V)\\
        &=X^H\omega(Y^H,Z^V)-Y^H\omega(X^H, Z^V)+Z^V\omega(X^H, Y^H)\\
        &=X^Hh(Y^H, Z^H)-Y^Hh(X^H, Z^H)+0,
    \end{align*}
    where the fact that~$Z^V\omega(X^H, Y^H)=0$ follows from
    the~$\mathbb{A}$-invariance.
<!-- end proof-16 -->
<!-- definition-14: body_md -->
We denote the quotient manifold 
    by~$M^\circ_\mathbb{A}:=N^\circ_\mathbb{A}/\mathbb{A}$,
    and the quotient map 
    by~$\pi\colon N^\circ_\mathbb{A}\rightarrow M^\circ_\mathbb{A}$.
    Moreover, for any~$X\in\mathfrak{a}$,
    we define a vector field~$X^B$ on~$M^\circ_\mathbb{A}$
    by~$X^B:=\pi_*X^H$.
<!-- end definition-14 -->
<!-- note-10: body_md -->
For any~$X,Y\in\mathfrak{a}$, we have~$[X^B, Y^B]=0$.
<!-- end note-10 -->
<!-- fact-8: body_md -->
\label{fac:OpenDense}
    Suppose that a connected abelian Lie group~$G$
    acts on a connected manifold~$N$ effectively and properly.
    Then,~$N^\circ:=\{p\in N~:~G_p=\{e\}\}$
    is an open and dense subset of~$N$.
    If~$N$ is orientable, then~$N^\circ$ is connected.
<!-- end fact-8 -->
<!-- note-11: body_md -->
\label{not:OpenDense}
    Since any complex manifold is orientable,
    by the Fact~\ref{fac:OpenDense},
    the subset~$N^\circ_\mathbb{A}\subset N$
    is open, dense and connected,
    and hence the quotient manifold~$M^\circ_\mathbb{A}$
    is connected.
<!-- end note-11 -->
<!-- lemma-8: body_md -->
\label{lem:FlatConnection}
    Let~$V\subset \mathfrak{X}(M)$ be 
    an~$n$-dimensional vector space
    of vector fields
    on an~$n$-dimensional manifold~$M$.
    If~$V$ satisfies the following conditions,
    then there exists a unique flat affine connection~$\nabla$
    satisfying~$V=\mathfrak{X}_\nabla(M):=
    \{X\in\mathfrak{X}(M)~:~\nabla X=0\}$.\\
    (i)~For any~$p\in M$,~$\{X_p\in T_pM~:~ X\in V\}=T_pM.$\\
    (ii)~For any~$X,Y\in V$,~$[X,Y]=0.$
<!-- end lemma-8 -->
<!-- proof-17: body_md -->
The affine connection~$\nabla$ on~$M$
    is uniquely determined by requiring
    $\nabla X=0$ for any~$X\in V$.
    Then, the torsion tensor~$T$ and curvature tensor~$R$ of~$\nabla$
    satisfy
    \begin{align*}
        T(X,Y)&=\nabla_XY-\nabla_YX-[X,Y]=0\\
        R(X,Y)Z&=\nabla_X\nabla_YZ-\nabla_Y\nabla_XZ-\nabla_{[X,Y]}Z=0
    \end{align*}
    for any~$X, Y, Z\in V$, and hence~$\nabla$ is flat.
<!-- end proof-17 -->
<!-- fact-9: body_md -->
\label{fac:RiemannianQuotient}
    If a Lie group~$G$ acts freely and properly on a manifold~$N$,
    then the quotient space~$N/G$ admits a unique smooth manifold structure
    such that the quotient map~$\pi\colon N\rightarrow N/G$
    is a submersion, and moreover, $N$ becomes a principal~$G$-bundle
    over~$N/G$.
    Furthermore, if~$N$ is a Riemannian manifold 
    and~$G$ acts by isometries, 
    then~$N/G$ admits a unique Riemannian metric making
    $\pi$ a Riemannian submersion.
    Here, a submersion~$f\colon N\rightarrow N'$ between Riemannian manifolds~$N$
    and~$N'$ is called a Riemannian submersion if, for every point~$p\in N$,
    the differential~
    \begin{equation*}
        (df)_p\colon (\operatorname{\mathrm{Ker}} (df)_p)^{\perp}\rightarrow T_{f(p)}N'
    \end{equation*}
    restricted to the subspace~$(\operatorname{\mathrm{Ker}} (df)_p)^{\perp}\subset T_pN$
    is an isometry.
<!-- end fact-9 -->
<!-- lemma-9: body_md -->
\label{lem:HorizontalDistribution}
    For any~$p\in N^\circ_\mathbb{A}$,
    we have
    \begin{align*}
        \ker{d\pi_p}&=\{X^V_p\in T_pN~:~ X\in\mathfrak{a}\}\\
        (\ker{d\pi_p})^\perp&=\{X^H_p\in T_pN~:~ X\in\mathfrak{a}\}.
    \end{align*}
<!-- end lemma-9 -->
<!-- proof-18: body_md -->
The first identity follows from
    $\ker d\pi_p=T_p(\mathbb{A}\cdot p)$.
    For the second identity,
    the inclusion~$\supset$ follows from~Lemma~\ref{lem:Lagrangeness}.
    Since, by the first identity, the map
    $\mathfrak{a}\rightarrow\ker{d\pi_p},~X\mapsto X^V_p$
    is a linear isomorphism,
    the vector space~$\{X^H_p\in T_pN~:~ X\in\mathfrak{a}\}$
    is~$n$-dimensional.
    Hence, the reverse inclusion~$\subset$ holds.
<!-- end proof-18 -->
<!-- proposition-11: body_md -->
\label{prop:QuotientHessian}
    There exist a unique Hessian structure~$(\nabla, g)$
    on~$M^\circ_\mathbb{A}$ satisfying the following conditions:\\
    (i)~$\pi$ is a Riemannian submersion.\\
    (ii)~For any~$X\in\mathfrak{a}$,~$\nabla X^B=0.$

    In this case, for any~$X, Y\in \mathfrak{a}$,
    we have
    \begin{equation*}
        h(X^H,Y^H)=h(X^V,Y^V)=g(X^B,Y^B)\circ \pi.
    \end{equation*}
<!-- end proposition-11 -->
<!-- proof-19: body_md -->
A flat affine connection~$\nabla$ and
    a Riemannian metric~$g$ on~$M^\circ_\mathbb{A}$
    are uniquely determined  by 
    Lemma~\ref{lem:FlatConnection}
    and
    Fact~\ref{fac:RiemannianQuotient}, respectively.
    The identity then follows from
    Lemma~\ref{lem:HorizontalDistribution}.
    Moreover, it follows from Fact~\ref{fac:HessianCondition} and 
    Lemma~\ref{lem:Lagrangeness}~(3)
    that~$(\nabla, g)$ defines a Hessian structure
    on~$M^\circ_\mathbb{A}$.
<!-- end proof-19 -->
<!-- note-12: body_md -->
\label{not:QuotientParallelVector}
    In this case,
    the map~$\mathfrak{a}\rightarrow \mathfrak{X}_\nabla(M^\circ_{\mathbb{A}}),~
    X\mapsto X^B$ is a linear isomorphism.
<!-- end note-12 -->
<!-- lemma-10: body_md -->
\label{lem:TangentBundleQuotient}
    For a Hessian domain~$U$, 
    suppose that the tangent bundle
    $TU\cong U\times \mathbb{R}^{n}$
    carries the K\"{a}hler~structure 
    and the effective, proper, free, and Hamiltonian~$\mathbb{R}^{n}$-action
    defined in Section~\ref{sec:TangentBundleKahler}.
    Then
    the quotient manifold~$(U\times \mathbb{R}^{n})/\mathbb{R}^{n}$ 
    is isomorphic to~$U$ as a Hessian manifold.
<!-- end lemma-10 -->
<!-- proof-20: body_md -->
By definition,
    the projection~$\mathrm{pr}_1\colon U\times \mathbb{R}^{n}\rightarrow U$
    induces a Hessian isomorphism
    $(U\times \mathbb{R}^{n})/\mathbb{R}^{n}\rightarrow U$
    via the 
    quotient map~$\pi\colon U\times \mathbb{R}^{n}\rightarrow (U\times \mathbb{R}^{n})/\mathbb{R}^{n}$.
<!-- end proof-20 -->
<!-- definition-15: body_md -->
For~$(N,\mathbb{A})$ and~$(N',\mathbb{A}')$, 
    let~$F\colon N\rightarrow N'$ be an isomorphism of K\"{a}hler~manifolds 
    and let~$\rho\colon\mathbb{A}\rightarrow\mathbb{A}'$ be a Lie group isomorphism. 
    We say that~$F$ is an equivariant isomorphism with respect to~$\rho$
    if~$F\circ a=\rho(a)\circ F$ for every~$a\in\mathbb{A}$.
<!-- end definition-15 -->
<!-- lemma-11: body_md -->
\label{lem:QuotientMorphism}
    For~$(N,\mathbb{A})$ and~$(N',\mathbb{A}')$,
    suppose that
    a local diffeomorphism~$F\colon N\rightarrow N'$
    preserving the K\"{a}hler~structures
    and a surjective Lie group homomorphism
    $\rho\colon \mathbb{A}\rightarrow \mathbb{A}'$
    satisfy~$F(N^\circ_{\mathbb{A}})\subset
    (N')^\circ_{\mathbb{A}'}$
    and~$F\circ a=\rho(a)\circ F$ for every~$a\in\mathbb{A}$.
    Then, there exists a local diffeomorphism
    $f\colon M^\circ_{\mathbb{A}}\rightarrow (M')^\circ_{\mathbb{A}'}$
    preserving the Hessian structures such that
    $f\circ\pi =\pi'\circ F$,
    where~$\pi\colon N^\circ_{\mathbb{A}}\rightarrow M^\circ_{\mathbb{A}}$
    and~$\pi'\colon (N')^\circ_{\mathbb{A}'}\rightarrow
    (M')^\circ_{\mathbb{A}'}$ denote the quotient maps.
<!-- end lemma-11 -->
<!-- proof-21: body_md -->
Since, by the condition~$F\circ a=\rho(a)\circ F$,
    $F$ sends~$\mathbb{A}$-orbits to
    $\mathbb{A}'$-orbits,
    there exists a map
    $f\colon M^\circ_{\mathbb{A}}\rightarrow (M')^\circ_{\mathbb{A}'}$
    such that~$f\circ\pi =\pi'\circ F$.
    Moreover, for any~$p\in N$ and~$X\in \mathfrak{a}$,
    \begin{equation*}
        F_*X^V_p
        =\left.\frac{d}{dt}F(\exp(tX)\cdot p)\right|_{t=0}
        =\left.\frac{d}{dt}\rho(\exp(tX))\cdot F(p)\right|_{t=0}
        =(\rho_*X)^V_{F(p)}.
    \end{equation*}
    Hence, we have~$F_*X^V=(\rho_*X)^V$ and~$F_*X^H=(\rho_*X)^H$,
    together with~$f_*X^B=(\rho_*X)^B$.
    Thus, by Note~\ref{not:QuotientParallelVector},
    $f$ preserves the affine connections,
    since it sends parallel vector fields
    on~$M^\circ_{\mathbb{A}}$
    to parallel vector fields on~$(M')^\circ_{\mathbb{A}'}$.
    Moreover,~$f$ preserves the Riemannian metrics
    by Lemma~\ref{lem:Lagrangeness} and
    Proposition~\ref{prop:QuotientHessian}.
    Therefore,~$f$ is a local diffeomorphism preserving
    the Hessian structures.
<!-- end proof-21 -->
<!-- lemma-12: body_md -->
\label{lem:FreeSubset}
    For~$(N,\mathbb{A})$ and~$(N',\mathbb{A}')$, 
    let~$F:N\rightarrow N'$ 
    be an equivariant isomorphism
    with respect to a Lie group isomorphism
    $\rho\colon \mathbb{A}\rightarrow \mathbb{A}'$.
    Then, we have~$F(N^\circ_{\mathbb{A}})=(N')^\circ_{\mathbb{A}'}.$
<!-- end lemma-12 -->
<!-- proof-22: body_md -->
The claim follows from
    $\rho(\mathbb{A}_p)=\mathbb{A}'_{F(p)}$
    for any~$p\in N^\circ_{\mathbb{A}}$.
<!-- end proof-22 -->
<!-- proposition-12: body_md -->
\label{prop:QuotientIsomorphism}
    For~$(N,\mathbb{A})$ and~$(N',\mathbb{A}')$, 
    let~$F:N\rightarrow N'$ 
    be an equivariant isomorphism
    with respect to a Lie group isomorphism
    $\rho\colon \mathbb{A}\rightarrow \mathbb{A}'$.
    Then, there exists an isomorphism
    $f\colon M^\circ_{\mathbb{A}}\rightarrow (M')^\circ_{\mathbb{A}'}$
    of Hessian manifolds
    such that
    $f\circ\pi =\pi'\circ F$,
    where~$\pi\colon N^\circ_{\mathbb{A}}\rightarrow M^\circ_{\mathbb{A}}$
    and~$\pi'\colon (N')^\circ_{\mathbb{A}'}\rightarrow
    (M')^\circ_{\mathbb{A}'}$ denote the quotient maps.
<!-- end proposition-12 -->
<!-- proof-23: body_md -->
Since, by Lemma~\ref{lem:FreeSubset}, 
    $F$ and~$\rho$ satisfy the conditions 
    in Lemma~\ref{lem:QuotientMorphism},
    there exists a local diffeomorphism
    $f\colon M^\circ_{\mathbb{A}}\rightarrow (M')^\circ_{\mathbb{A}'}$
    preserving the Hessian structures,
    which is in fact a diffeomorphism
    since~$F$ is invertible.
<!-- end proof-23 -->
<!-- fact-10: body_md -->
\label{fac:IsometryExtension}
    Any isometry locally defined on connected open subsets of
    connected, simply connected, complete and analytic
    Riemannian manifolds
    extends uniquely to a global isometry.
<!-- end fact-10 -->
<!-- note-13: body_md -->
\label{not:LocalIsomorphismExtension}
    Any isomorphism of K\"{a}hler~manifolds 
    locally defined on connected open subsets of
    connected, simply connected, complete and analytic
    K\"{a}hler~manifolds
    extends uniquely to a global isomorphism
    of K\"{a}hler~manifolds.
    Indeed, the extension to a global isometry given 
    by Fact~\ref{fac:IsometryExtension}
    is globally holomorphic.
<!-- end note-13 -->
<!-- proposition-13: body_md -->
\label{prop:HessianKahlerIsomorphism}
    For~$(N,\mathbb{A})$ and~$(N',\mathbb{A}')$,
    if~$N$ and~$N'$ are connected, simply connected,
    complete and analytic, then for any isomorphism 
    of Hessian manifolds
    $f\colon M^\circ_{\mathbb{A}}\rightarrow
    (M')^\circ_{\mathbb{A}'}$,
    there exists an equivariant isomorphism
    $F\colon N\rightarrow N'$ with respect to~
    a Lie group isomorphism~$\rho\colon
    \mathbb{A}\rightarrow \mathbb{A}'$
    such that~$\pi'\circ F=f\circ\pi$,
    where~$\pi\colon N^\circ_{\mathbb{A}}\rightarrow M^\circ_{\mathbb{A}}$
    and~$\pi'\colon (N')^\circ_{\mathbb{A}'}\rightarrow
    (M')^\circ_{\mathbb{A}'}$ denote the quotient maps.
<!-- end proposition-13 -->
<!-- proof-24: body_md -->
Put~$M:=M^\circ_{\mathbb{A}}$ and~$M':=(M')^\circ_{\mathbb{A}'}$.
    By Note~\ref{not:OpenDense}, 
    $M$ and~$M'$ are connected. 
    Since~$f\colon M\rightarrow M'$ is affine, 
    Note~\ref{not:QuotientParallelVector} implies 
    that there exists a linear isomorphism
    $R\colon\mathfrak{a}\rightarrow\mathfrak{a}'$ s
    uch that~$f_*X^B=(RX)^B$ for any~$X\in\mathfrak{a}$.
    Moreover, since~$f$ is an isometry, we have
    $g'((RX)^B,(RY)^B)\circ f=g(X^B,Y^B)$
    for any~$X,Y\in\mathfrak{a}$.

    First, we show that an isomorphism~$F$ 
    of K\"{a}hler~manifolds exists locally. 
    Fix~$p\in N^\circ_{\mathbb{A}}$ 
    and~$p'\in\pi'^{-1}(f(p))\subset (N')^\circ_{\mathbb{A}'}$. 
    Since~$\mathfrak{a}$ and~$\mathfrak{a}'$ are abelian, 
    there exist open neighborhoods~$W\subset N^\circ_{\mathbb{A}}$ 
    and~$W'\subset (N')^\circ_{\mathbb{A}'}$ of~$p$ and~$p'$, respectively, 
    and a smooth map~$F\colon W\rightarrow W'$ such that~$F(p)=p'$ and
    $F_*X^V=(RX)^V,~F_*X^H=(RX)^H$ for any~$X\in\mathfrak{a}$.
    Then,~$\pi'\circ F,f\circ\pi\colon W\rightarrow M'$ 
    both send~$p$ to~$f(p)$ 
    and~$X^H,X^V$ to~$(RX)^H,0$, respectively. 
    Hence, we have~$\pi'\circ F=f\circ\pi$.
    Therefore, by Lemma~\ref{lem:Lagrangeness} 
    and Proposition~\ref{prop:QuotientHessian}, 
    $F$ is an isomorphism of K\"{a}hler~manifolds.

    Next, we show that~$F$ extends globally and 
    is an equivariant isomorphism with respect to some~$\rho$.
    By Note~\ref{not:LocalIsomorphismExtension}, 
    $F$ extends to a map~$N\rightarrow N'$ preserving the 
    K\"{a}hler~structures, and the invertibility of~$f$ implies 
    that~$F$ is an isomorphism. Moreover, by analyticity, we have
    $F_*X^V=(RX)^V,~F_*X^H=(RX)^H$ on~$N$.
    Then, for any~$p\in N^\circ_{\mathbb{A}}$ 
    and~$X\in\mathfrak{a}$, the uniqueness of integral curves gives
    \begin{equation*}
        F(\exp X\cdot p)=\exp(RX)\cdot F(p).
    \end{equation*}
    Hence, if~$\exp X=\exp Y$ for~$X,Y\in\mathfrak{a}$, 
    then~$\exp(RX)=\exp(RY)$. 
    Therefore,~$R$ induces a Lie group isomorphism
    $\rho\colon\mathbb{A}\rightarrow\mathbb{A}'$.
    Thus, again by the uniqueness of integral curves, 
    $F$ is equivariant with respect to~$\rho$. 
    By the same argument as on~$W$, we then have~$\pi'\circ F=f\circ\pi$.
<!-- end proof-24 -->
<!-- remark-4: body_md -->
In general,~$F$ is not unique, 
    since it can be composed with a translation 
    by an arbitrary element of~$\mathbb{A}$.
<!-- end remark-4 -->
<!-- corollary-2: body_md -->
\label{cor:IsomorphismEquivalence}
    Let~$N, N'$ be $2n$-dimensional
    connected, simply connected, complete and analytic K\"{a}hler~manifolds
    equipped with effective proper Hamiltonian actions
    of~$n$-dimensional connected abelian Lie groups~$\mathbb{A},\mathbb{A}'$,
    respectively.
    Then, the following conditions are equivalent:\\
    (a)~$(N, \mathbb{A})$ and~$(N', \mathbb{A}')$ are equivariantly isomorphic.\\
    (b)~$M^\circ_{\mathbb{A}}$ and~$(M')^\circ_{\mathbb{A}'}$ are
        isomorphic as Hessian manifolds.
<!-- end corollary-2 -->
<!-- proof-25: body_md -->
The implications in each direction follow from
    Propositions~\ref{prop:QuotientIsomorphism}~and
    \ref{prop:HessianKahlerIsomorphism}, respectively.
<!-- end proof-25 -->
<!-- note-14: body_md -->
\label{not:ClosedSubgroup}
    An effective proper action of a Lie group~$H$ on~$N$ 
    preserving the K\"{a}hler~structure induces an embedding of~$H$ 
    into~$G$ as a closed subgroup.
    Conversely, every closed subgroup~$H\subset G$ 
    naturally defines an effective proper action on~$N$ 
    preserving the K\"{a}hler~structure(\cite[Proposition 3.62]{AB15}).
<!-- end note-14 -->
<!-- proposition-14: body_md -->
Let~$N=(N,I,h,\omega)$ be a~$2n$-dimensional 
    connected, simply connected, complete, and analytic 
    K\"{a}hler~manifold,
    and denote the automorphism group of~$N$
    by~$G:=\operatorname{\mathrm{Aut}}(N)$.
    Suppose that a connected abelian closed subgroup
    $\mathbb{A}, \mathbb{A}'\subset G$
    defines (effective proper) Hamiltonian actions on~$N$.
    Then, the following conditions are equivalent:
    (a)~$\mathbb{A}$ and~$\mathbb{A}'$ are conjugate in~$G$.\\
    (b)~$(N,\mathbb{A})$ and~$(N',\mathbb{A}')$ are equivariantly isomorphic.\\
    (c)~The quotient Hessian manifolds~$M^\circ_{\mathbb{A}}$ and~$M^\circ_{\mathbb{A}'}$ 
    are isomorphic as Hessian manifolds.
<!-- end proposition-14 -->
<!-- proof-26: body_md -->
The equivalence~$(a)\Leftrightarrow(b)$ follows 
    from the fact that the existence of~$F\in G$ satisfying
    $F\mathbb{A}F^{-1}=\mathbb{A}'$
    is equivalent to the fact that~$F$ is 
    an equivariant isomorphism with respect to the Lie group isomorphism
    $\rho\colon \mathbb{A}\rightarrow\mathbb{A}',~
    a\mapsto FaF^{-1}$.
    The equivalence~$(b)\Leftrightarrow(c)$ follows 
    from Corollary~\ref{cor:IsomorphismEquivalence}.
<!-- end proof-26 -->
<!-- example-3: body_md -->
\label{exm:ComplexSpaceForms}
    (1)~Let~$C>0$.
    The complex projective space
    $\mathbb{C}P^n:=(\mathbb{C}^n\setminus\{0\})/\mathbb{C}^\times$
    is naturally a K\"{a}hler~manifold
    with respect to the Riemannian metric~$h_{\mathrm{std}}$,
    called the Fubini-Study metric.
    In the complex chart
    on~$U_{n+1}:=\{[\alpha^1:\cdots :\alpha^{n+1}]
    \in\mathbb{C}P^n~:~\alpha^{n+1}\neq 0\}$
    given by
    $U_{n+1}\rightarrow \mathbb{C}^{n},~[\alpha^1:\cdots :\alpha^{n+1}]\mapsto 
    z:=\left(\frac{\alpha^1}{\alpha^{n+1}}
    ,\ldots, \frac{\alpha^n}{\alpha^{n+1}}\right)$,
    $h_{\mathrm{std}}$ is expressed as
    \begin{equation*}
        h_{\mathrm{std}}=2\left(\frac{\delta_{ij}}{1+\|z\|^2}
        -\frac{\bar{z}^iz^j}{(1+\|z\|^2)^2}\right)
        (dz^i \otimes d\bar{z}^j+d\bar{z}^j\otimes dz^i).
    \end{equation*}
    Moreover, the function~$\Psi\colon U_{n+1}\rightarrow \mathbb{R}^{}$
    given by
    \begin{equation*}
        \Psi=4\log (1+\|z\|^2)
    \end{equation*}
    is a K\"{a}hler~potential on~$U_{n+1}$.\\
    (2)~The complex Euclidean space~$\mathbb{C}^{n}$
    is a K\"{a}hler~manifold
    with respect to the
    Euclidean metric~$h_{\mathrm{std}}$.
    Moreover, the function~$\Psi\colon \mathbb{C}^{n}\rightarrow \mathbb{R}^{}$
    given by
    \begin{equation*}
        \Psi=4\|z\|^2
    \end{equation*}
    is a K\"{a}hler~potential on~$\mathbb{C}^{n}$.\\
    (3)~Let~$C<0$.
    The open unit ball~$D_n=\{z\in \mathbb{C}^{n}~:~\|z\|<1\}$
    is a K\"{a}hler~manifold
    with respect to the
    Riemannian metric~$h_{\mathrm{std}}$ given by
    \begin{equation*}
        h_\mathrm{std}=2\left(\frac{\delta_{ij}}{1-\|z\|^2}
        -\frac{\bar{z}^iz^j}{(1-\|z\|^2)^2}\right)
        (dz^i \otimes d\bar{z}^j+d\bar{z}^j\otimes dz^i).
    \end{equation*}
    Moreover, the function~$\Psi\colon D_n\rightarrow \mathbb{R}^{}$
    given by
    \begin{equation*}
        \Psi=-4\log (1-\|z\|^2)
    \end{equation*}
    is a K\"{a}hler~potential on~$D_n$.\\
<!-- end example-3 -->
<!-- proposition-15: body_md -->
\label{prop:Section4}
    Let $c\in\mathbb{R}^{}$.\\
    (1)~The K\"{a}hler~manifold
    $N:=\begin{cases}
    \mathbb{C}P^n &(c<0)\\
    \mathbb{C}^n  &(c=0)\\
    D_n  & (c>0)
    \end{cases}$
    with metric
    $\begin{cases}
    \frac{1}{|c|}h_{\mathrm{std}} &(c<0)\\
    h_{\mathrm{std}} &(c=0)\\
    \frac{1}{|c|}h_{\mathrm{std}}  & (c>0)
    \end{cases}$
    has automorphism group
    $G:=\operatorname{\mathrm{Aut}}(N)\cong\begin{cases}
    PU(n+1) &(c<0)\\
    U(n)\ltimes \mathbb{C}^{n} &(c=0)\\
    PU(n,1)  & (c>0)
    \end{cases}$.
    Every~$n$-dimensional connected abelian 
    subgroup~$\mathbb{A}\subset G$ 
    whose action on~$N$ generates an isotropic subspace 
    at some point in~$N$ is conjugate to one of
    $\begin{cases}
        \mathbb{A}_-^n &(c<0)\\
        \mathbb{A}_0^{n,k}~(k=0,\ldots, n)&(c=0)\\
        \mathbb{A}_+^{n},
        \mathbb{A}_+^{n,\mathrm{H}},
        \mathbb{A}_+^{n,k}~(k=1,\ldots,n)& (c>0)
    \end{cases}$
    and, in particular,~$\mathbb{A}$ is a closed subgroup.\\
    (2)~The subgroup~$\mathbb{A}\subset G$ given above induces an
    effective proper Hamiltonian action on~$N$, and the
    quotient manifold is, respectively, isomorphic as a Hessian manifold to
    $M^\circ_{\mathbb{A}}\cong\begin{cases}
        \mathcal{S}_-^n(c) &(c<0)\\
        \mathcal{R}_0^{n,k}(0)~(k=0,\ldots, n)&(c=0)\\
        \mathcal{H}_+^{n}(c),
        \mathcal{H}_+^{n,\mathrm{H}}(c),
        \mathcal{H}_+^{n,k}(c)~(k=1,\ldots,n)& (c>0)
    \end{cases}$.
<!-- end proposition-15 -->
<!-- proof-27: body_md -->
(1)~For~$c>0$,~$c=0$, and~$c<0$, 
    the claim is the same statement as 
    Note~\ref{not:PositiveAbelianSubgroup}, 
    Lemma~\ref{lem:ZeroAbelianSubgroup} and 
    Note~\ref{fac:NegativeAbelianSubgroup}, respectively.

(2)~For~$c>0$,~$c=0$, and~$c<0$, 
    the claim is the same statement as  
    Propositions~\ref{prop:PositiveQuotient}, 
    \ref{prop:ZeroQuotient} and \ref{prop:NegativeQuotient}, respectively.
<!-- end proof-27 -->
<!-- note-15: body_md -->
For the K\"{a}hler~manifold~$N=\mathbb{C}P^n$, 
    the automorphism group~$G$ 
    is given by the action of~$PU(n+1)$ 
    on~$\mathbb{C}P^n$ induced by matrix multiplication.
<!-- end note-15 -->
<!-- definition-16: body_md -->
\label{def:PositiveAbelianSubgroups}
    We define an~$n$-dimensional connected abelian closed subgroup
    $\mathbb{A}_-^n\subset PU(n+1)$
    as follows:
    \begin{equation*}
        \mathbb{A}_-^n
        :=\left\{
            \left[\begin{pmatrix}
                a&  \\
                & 1
            \end{pmatrix}\right]\in PU(n+1)
        ~:~
        a\in U(1)^{n}\right\}.
    \end{equation*}
    Then,~$\mathfrak{a}_-^n:=\mathrm{Lie}(\mathbb{A}_-^n)$
    is given by
    \begin{equation*}
        \mathfrak{a}_-^n
        =\left\{
            \left[\begin{pmatrix}
                X&  \\
                & 0
            \end{pmatrix}\right]
        ~:~
        X\in \mathfrak{u}(1)^{n} \right\}.
    \end{equation*}
<!-- end definition-16 -->
<!-- note-16: body_md -->
\label{not:PositiveAbelianSubgroup}
    $\mathbb{A}_-^n$ is the unique maximal torus of~$PU(n+1)$.
    Therefore, every~$n$-dimensional 
    connected abelian subgroup of~$PU(n+1)$ 
    is conjugate to~$\mathbb{A}_-^n$.
<!-- end note-16 -->
<!-- lemma-13: body_md -->
\label{lem:PositiveQuotient}
    Let~$C>0$. Set~$N:=\mathbb{C}P^n$ equipped with
    the metric~$\frac{1}{C}h_{\mathrm{std}}$,
    and let
    $\mathbb{A}:=\mathbb{A}_-^n\subset PU(n+1)$.
    Then the map~$\mu\colon N\rightarrow
    \mathfrak{a}^*\cong\mathbb{R}^n$ defined by
    \begin{equation*}
        \mu([\alpha^1:\cdots:\alpha^{n+1}])
        :=-\frac{1}{C\|\alpha\|^2}
        (|\alpha^1|^2,\ldots,|\alpha^n|^2)
    \end{equation*}
    is a moment map.
    Here, we identify~$\mathfrak{a}$ with~$\mathbb{R}^n$
    via the basis
    $\left(\frac{\sqrt{-1}}{2}E_{11},\ldots,
    \frac{\sqrt{-1}}{2}E_{nn}\right)$ of~$\mathfrak{a}$,
    where~$E_{ii}$ denotes the matrix unit.
<!-- end lemma-13 -->
<!-- proof-28: body_md -->
It suffices to consider the case~$C=1$.
    Moreover, by Note~\ref{not:OpenDense}, 
    it suffices to show that
    the restriction of~$\mu$ to
    $N^\circ_\mathbb{A}=\{[\alpha^1:\cdots:\alpha^{n+1}]\in N ~:~
    \forall i,~\alpha^i\neq 0\}$
    is a moment map.
    We use Proposition~\ref{prop:MomentMaps}.

    For the Hessian manifold~$\mathcal{S}^n(-1)$ defined in
    Example~\ref{exm:StandardModels}, let
    $N':=\mathcal{S}^n(-1)\times\mathbb{R}^n$ be equipped with the
    K\"{a}hler~structure in Fact~\ref{fac:TangentBundleKahler} and the
    effective proper Hamiltonian~$\mathbb{R}^n$-action in
    Proposition~\ref{prop:TangentMomentMap}.
    We denote by~$\Psi'$ and~$\mu'$ the K\"{a}hler~potential and moment map,
    respectively, on~$N'$ defined in
    Example~\ref{exm:StandardModelsKahler}.
    Using the complex chart~$(w^1,\ldots,w^n)$ on~$N'$ from
    Note~\ref{not:TangentHolomorphicChart}, define
    \begin{equation*}
        F\colon N'\rightarrow N^\circ_\mathbb{A}
        \subset\mathbb{C}P^n,~
        (w^1,\ldots, w^n)\mapsto \left[e^\frac{w^1}{2}:\cdots
        :e^{\frac{w^n}{2}}:1\right].
    \end{equation*}
    We also define the surjective homomorphism
    $\rho\colon\mathbb{R}^n\rightarrow\mathbb{A}$ by
    \begin{equation*}
        \rho\colon \mathbb{R}^{n}\rightarrow \mathbb{A}\subset PU(n+1),~
        (a^1,\ldots,a^n)\mapsto 
        \left[\begin{pmatrix}
            e^{ \frac{\sqrt{-1}}{2}a^1}& & & \\
             &\ddots& & \\
             & &e^{\frac{\sqrt{-1}}{2}a^n}&\\
             & & &1
        \end{pmatrix}
        \right].
    \end{equation*}
    It therefore suffices to show that~$F$ is a surjective local
    diffeomorphism preserving the K\"{a}hler~structures, and that
    $F$,~$\rho$,~$\mu'$ and~$\mu$ satisfy conditions~(i) and~(ii) of
    Proposition~\ref{prop:MomentMaps}.

    Conditions~(i) and~(ii) follow by direct computation.
    Moreover,~$N^\circ_{\mathbb{A}}\subset U_{n+1}$ 
    (see Example~\ref{exm:ComplexSpaceForms}), and the K\"{a}hler~potential
    $\Psi:=4\log(1+\|z\|^2)$
    on~$U_{n+1}\subset N$ satisfies
    $\Psi\circ F-\Psi'=0$.
    Hence, by Note~\ref{not:KahlerPotentialDifference},
    $F$ preserves the K\"{a}hler~structures.
    The inverse of~$F$ is locally given by
    \begin{equation*}
        N^\circ_\mathbb{A}\rightarrow N',~
        (z^1,\ldots, z^n)\mapsto (2\log z^1,\ldots, 2\log z^n),
    \end{equation*}
    where a branch of~$\log$ is chosen appropriately. 
    Therefore,~$F$ is a surjective local diffeomorphism.
<!-- end proof-28 -->
<!-- proposition-16: body_md -->
\label{prop:PositiveQuotient}
    Let~$C>0$.
    Set~$N:=\mathbb{C}P^n$ with~$\frac{1}{C}h_{\mathrm{std}}$ and
    $\mathbb{A}:=\mathbb{A}_-^n\subset PU(n+1)$.\\
    (1)~$\mathbb{A}$ naturally induces a Hamiltonian action on~$N$.\\
    (2)~As Hessian manifolds,~$M^\circ_\mathbb{A}:=N_\mathbb{A}^\circ/\mathbb{A}
    \cong \mathcal{S}^n(-C)$.
<!-- end proposition-16 -->
<!-- proof-29: body_md -->
We use the maps~$F$,~$\rho$,~$\mu$ and~$\mu'$ defined in
    Lemma~\ref{lem:PositiveQuotient} and its proof.

    (1) follows immediately from Lemma~\ref{lem:PositiveQuotient}.
    For (2), 
    by Lemma~\ref{lem:QuotientMorphism}, 
    it suffices to show
    that the local diffeomorphism
    $f\colon \mathcal{S}^n(-C)\rightarrow M^\circ_\mathbb{A}$
    induced by~$F$ is bijective.

    Surjectivity follows from the surjectivity of~$F$.
    To prove injectivity, by Lemma~\ref{lem:QuotientMorphism}, 
    we have
    $\pi(F(p,0))=f(p)$.
    Thus, for arbitrary $p,q\in\mathcal{S}^n(-C)$, if
    $f(p)=f(q)$, then
    $\pi(F(p,0))=\pi(F(q,0))$.
    Since~$\mu$ is~$\mathbb{A}$-invariant, this implies
    $\mu(F(p,0))=\mu(F(q,0)).$
    On the other hand, the map
    $\mathcal{S}^n(-C)\rightarrow
    \mathfrak{a}^*,~p\mapsto \mu(F(p,0))$
    is given by
    \begin{equation*}
        (\theta^1,\ldots,\theta^n)\mapsto-\frac{1}{C}\left(\frac{e^{\theta^1}}{1+e^{\theta^1}
    +\cdots+e^{\theta^n}},\ldots,
    \frac{e^{\theta^n}}{1+e^{\theta^1}
    +\cdots+e^{\theta^n}}\right),
    \end{equation*}
    which is injective by a direct computation. 
    Hence~$f$ is injective. Therefore,~$f$ is bijective.
<!-- end proof-29 -->
<!-- note-17: body_md -->
For the K\"{a}hler~manifold~$N=\mathbb{C}^n$ 
    equipped with the Euclidean metric, 
    the automorphism group is
    $G\cong U(n)\ltimes\mathbb{C}^n$, 
    acting by affine transformations.
<!-- end note-17 -->
<!-- definition-17: body_md -->
\label{def:ZeroAbelianSubgroups}
    For~$k=0, \ldots, n$,
    we define~$n$-dimensional connected abelian closed
    subgroups
    $\mathbb{A}_0^{n,k}$ as follows:
    \begin{equation*}
        \mathbb{A}_0^{n,k}
        :=\left\{\left(
            \begin{pmatrix}
                1&  \\
                & a \\
            \end{pmatrix},
            \begin{pmatrix}
                b\\
                0
            \end{pmatrix}
            \right)
            \in U(n)\ltimes\mathbb{C}^{n}
        ~:~
        a\in U(1)^{n-k},~b\in \mathbb{R}^{k} \right\}.
    \end{equation*}
    Then,~$\mathfrak{a}_0^{n,k}:=\mathrm{Lie}(\mathbb{A}_0^{n,k})$
    is given by
    \begin{equation*}
        \mathfrak{a}_0^{n,k}=
        \left\{\left(
            \begin{pmatrix}
            0&  \\
                & X \\
            \end{pmatrix},
            \begin{pmatrix}
                y\\
                0
            \end{pmatrix}
            \right)
        ~:~
        X\in\mathfrak{u}(1)^{n-k},~y\in \mathbb{R}^{k} \right\}.
    \end{equation*}
<!-- end definition-17 -->
<!-- lemma-14: body_md -->
\label{lem:ZeroQuotient}
    Let~$N:=\mathbb{C}^{n}$ with Euclidean metric,
    and let~$\mathbb{A}:=\mathbb{A}_0^{n,k}$.
    Then, the map~$\mu\colon N\rightarrow \mathfrak{a}^*\cong\mathbb{R}^{n}$
    defined by
    \begin{equation*}
        \mu(z^1,\ldots,z^n):=(2\Im z^1,\ldots,2\Im z^k, -|z^{k+1}|^2,
        \ldots,-|z^n|^2)
    \end{equation*}
    is a moment map.
    Here, we identify~$\mathfrak{a}$ with~$\mathbb{R}^{n}$
    via the basis
    \begin{equation*}
        \left(
    \frac{1}{2}
    (0, e_1),\ldots
    \frac{1}{2}(0, e_k),
    \frac{\sqrt{-1}}{2}\left(
        E_{(k+1)(k+1)}, 0
    \right),
    \ldots,
    \frac{\sqrt{-1}}{2}\left(E_{nn}, 0
    \right)\right)
    \end{equation*}
    of~$\mathfrak{a}$,
    where~$e_i$ denotes the standard basis of~$\mathbb{R}^{n}$,
    and~$E_{ii}$ denotes the matrix unit.
<!-- end lemma-14 -->
<!-- proof-30: body_md -->
By Note~\ref{not:OpenDense},
    it suffices to show that the
    restriction of~$\mu$ to~$N_\mathbb{A}^\circ=\{(z^1,\ldots,z^n)
    \in\mathbb{C}^{n}~:~ z^{k+1},\ldots, z^n\neq 0\}$
    is a moment map.
    We use Proposition~\ref{prop:MomentMaps}.

    For the Hessian manifold~$\mathcal{R}^{n,k}(0)$ defined in
    Example~\ref{exm:StandardModels}, let
    $N':=\mathcal{R}^{n,k}(0)\times\mathbb{R}^n$ be equipped with the
    K\"{a}hler~structure in Fact~\ref{fac:TangentBundleKahler} and the
    effective proper Hamiltonian~$\mathbb{R}^n$-action in
    Proposition~\ref{prop:TangentMomentMap}.
    We denote by~$\Psi'$ and~$\mu'$ the K\"{a}hler~potential and moment map,
    respectively, on~$N'$ defined in
    Example~\ref{exm:StandardModelsKahler}.
    Using the complex chart~$(w^1,\ldots,w^n)$ on~$N'$ from
    Note~\ref{not:TangentHolomorphicChart}, define
    \begin{equation*}
        F\colon N'\rightarrow N^\circ_\mathbb{A}
        \subset \mathbb{C}^{n},~
        (w^1,\ldots, w^n)\mapsto \left(-\frac{\sqrt{-1}}{2}w^1,\ldots,
        -\frac{\sqrt{-1}}{2}w^k, e^\frac{w^{k+1}}{2},\ldots,
        e^\frac{w^{n}}{2}\right).
    \end{equation*}
    We also define the surjective homomorphism
    $\rho\colon\mathbb{R}^n\rightarrow\mathbb{A}$ by
    \begin{equation*}
        \rho\colon \mathbb{R}^{n}\rightarrow \mathbb{A},~
        (a^1,\ldots,a^n)\mapsto 
        \left(
        \begin{pmatrix}
            1 & & & & & \\
             & \ddots& && & \\
             & &1 & & & \\
             & & &e^{\frac{\sqrt{-1}}{2}a^{k+1}}& & \\
             & & & &\ddots& \\
             & & & & &e^{\frac{\sqrt{-1}}{2}a^n} 
        \end{pmatrix},
        \begin{pmatrix}
            \frac{a^1}{2}\\ \vdots\\ \frac{a^k}{2}\\
            0 \\ \vdots\\ 0
        \end{pmatrix}
        \right).
    \end{equation*}
    It therefore suffices to show that~$F$ is a surjective local
    diffeomorphism preserving the K\"{a}hler~structures, and that
    $F$,~$\rho$,~$\mu'$ and~$\mu$ satisfy conditions~(i) and~(ii) of
    Proposition~\ref{prop:MomentMaps}.

    Conditions~(i) and~(ii) follow by direct computation.
    Moreover,~the K\"{a}hler~potential
    $\Psi:=4\|z\|^2$
    on~$N$ satisfies
    \begin{equation*}
        \Psi\circ F-\Psi'=-\frac{1}{2}((w^1)^2+\cdots+(w^k)^2)
        -\frac{1}{2}
        ((\bar{w}^1)^2+\cdots+(\bar{w}^k)^2)
    \end{equation*}.
    Hence, by Note~\ref{not:KahlerPotentialDifference},
    $F$ preserves the K\"{a}hler~structures.
    The inverse of~$F$ is locally given by
    \begin{equation*}
        N^\circ_\mathbb{A}\rightarrow N',~
        (z^1,\ldots, z^n)\mapsto (2\sqrt{-1} z^1,\ldots, 2\sqrt{-1} z^k,
        2\log z^{k+1},\ldots, 2\log z^n).
    \end{equation*}
    where a branch of~$\log$ is chosen appropriately. 
    Therefore,~$F$ is a surjective local diffeomorphism.
<!-- end proof-30 -->
<!-- proposition-17: body_md -->
\label{prop:ZeroQuotient}
    Set~$k=0,\ldots, n$,
    Let~$N:=\mathbb{C}^{n}$ with Euclidean metric,
    and let
    $\mathbb{A}:=\mathbb{A}_0^{n,k}\subset U(n)\ltimes\mathbb{C}^{n}$.\\
    (1)~$\mathbb{A}$ naturally induces a Hamiltonian action on~$N$.\\
    (2)~As Hessian manifolds,~$M^\circ_\mathbb{A}:=
    N_\mathbb{A}^\circ/\mathbb{A}
    \cong \mathcal{R}^{n,k}(0)$.
<!-- end proposition-17 -->
<!-- proof-31: body_md -->
We use the maps~$F$,~$\rho$,~$\mu$ and~$\mu'$ defined in
    Lemma~\ref{lem:ZeroQuotient} and its proof.

    (1) follows immediately from Lemma~\ref{lem:ZeroQuotient}.
    For (2), 
    by Lemma~\ref{lem:QuotientMorphism}, 
    it suffices to show
    that the local diffeomorphism
    $f\colon \mathcal{R}^{n,k}(0)\rightarrow M^\circ_\mathbb{A}$
    induced by~$F$ is bijective.

    Surjectivity follows from the surjectivity of~$F$.
    To prove injectivity, by Lemma~\ref{lem:QuotientMorphism}, 
    we have
    $\pi(F(p,0))=f(p)$.
    Thus, for arbitrary $p,q\in\mathcal{R}^{n,k}(0)$, if
    $f(p)=f(q)$, then
    $\pi(F(p,0))=\pi(F(q,0))$.
    Since~$\mu$ is~$\mathbb{A}$-invariant, this implies
    $\mu(F(p,0))=\mu(F(q,0)).$
    On the other hand, the map
    $\mathcal{R}^{n,k}(0)\rightarrow
    \mathfrak{a}^*,~p\mapsto \mu(F(p,0))$
    is given by
    \begin{equation*}
        (\theta^1,\ldots,\theta^n)\mapsto -\left(\theta^1,\ldots,\theta^k,
    e^{\theta^{k+1}},\ldots, e^{\theta^n} \right)
    \end{equation*}
    which is injective by a direct computation. 
    Hence~$f$ is injective. Therefore,~$f$ is bijective.
<!-- end proof-31 -->
<!-- lemma-15: body_md -->
\label{lem:LagrangianSubspace}
    For any isotropic subspace~$V\subset\mathbb{C}^n$ 
    of the real vector space~$\mathbb{C}^n$ 
    with respect to the standard symplectic form
    $\omega\colon (v,w)\mapsto -\Im v^*w$,
    that is, a real vector subspace~$V\subset\mathbb{C}^{n}$
    satisfying~$\omega|_V=0$, 
    there exists some $a\in U(n)$ such that
    $aV\subset \mathbb{R}^{n}\subset \mathbb{C}^{n}$.
<!-- end lemma-15 -->
<!-- proof-32: body_md -->
Let~$V$ be an isotropic subspace. 
    Then~$\sqrt{-1} V\cap V={0}$. 
    Hence, an~$\mathbb{R}$-orthonormal basis 
    $(v_1,\ldots,v_m)$ of~$V$ with respect to 
    the standard real inner product~$(v,w)\mapsto \Re v^*w$ 
    is also a~$\mathbb{C}$-orthonormal system in~$\mathbb{C}^n$ 
    with respect to the standard Hermitian inner product 
    $(v,w)\mapsto v^*w$. Here,~$m:=\dim_{\mathbb{R}}V$.
    Thus, choose~$v_{m+1},\ldots,v_n\in\mathbb{C}^n$ 
    such that~$(v_1,\ldots,v_n)$ is a~$\mathbb{C}$-orthonormal 
    basis of~$\mathbb{C}^n$ with respect to the 
    standard Hermitian inner product, 
    and set~$u:=(v_1,\ldots,v_n)$. 
    Then~$u\in U(n)$ and~$u^{-1}V\subset\mathbb{R}^n$.
<!-- end proof-32 -->
<!-- note-18: body_md -->
For the action of~$G=U(n)\ltimes\mathbb{C}^n$ 
    on~$\mathbb{C}^n$, 
    the vector field generated by~$(X,y)\in\mathfrak{g}$ 
    is given, at~$z\in\mathbb{C}^n$, 
    by~$Xz+y$ 
    nder the natural identification~$T_z\mathbb{C}^n\cong\mathbb{C}^n$.
<!-- end note-18 -->
<!-- lemma-16: body_md -->
\label{lem:ZeroAbelianSubgroup}
    Let~$\mathbb{A}\subset G:=U(n)\ltimes\mathbb{C}^n$ 
    be an $n$-dimensional connected abelian subgroup. 
    If the action of~$\mathbb{A}$ generates 
    an isotropic subspace 
    at some point of~$N=\mathbb{C}^n$, 
    then~$\mathbb{A}$ is conjugate to 
    $\mathbb{A}_0^{n,k}$ for some $k=0,\ldots,n$.
<!-- end lemma-16 -->
<!-- proof-33: body_md -->
It suffices to show that the Lie algebra~$\mathfrak{a}$ 
    is conjugate to~$\mathfrak{a}_0^{n,k}$.
    Let~$p_1:\mathfrak{g}\rightarrow\mathfrak{u}(n)$ and 
    $p_2:\mathfrak{g}\rightarrow\mathbb{C}^n$ 
    denote the projections onto the 
    $\mathfrak{u}(n)$ and~$\mathbb{C}^n$, respectively. 
    Then,~$p_1$ is a Lie algebra homomorphism.

    First, we show the following claim:\\
    \textbf{Claim.}
    For any~$n$-dimensional 
    abelian subalgebra~$\mathfrak{a}\subset\mathfrak{g}$,
